STAGE 1 / LESSON 1

The JavaScript Workbench

Build a repeatable edit, run, inspect, explain loop.

Read: Ch. 1 · Introduction to JavaScript · §1.1–1.3
Suggested session: 55 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Separate the JavaScript language from its host environment.
  • Run and inspect a small program in a browser and Node.js.
  • Use predictions and evidence to debug a program.

One language, several environments

JavaScript defines values, expressions, objects, functions, and other language behavior. A host environment supplies additional capabilities. A browser provides a document and browser events; Node.js provides access to processes and files. The same arithmetic expression behaves similarly in both, but document.querySelector is a browser capability. Treating this distinction as a boundary helps you understand unfamiliar examples instead of memorizing where each function happens to work.

Create a scratch directory with one JavaScript file and one HTML file that loads it. Keep experiments small enough to inspect completely. Record how you ran each example, the expected output, and the actual output. When a name is missing, first identify whether it belongs to your code, the language, or the host. That question is often more useful than immediately changing syntax.

const minutes = 25;
const sessions = 4;
console.log({ totalMinutes: minutes * sessions });

Read programs as a sequence of observations

Before running a snippet, predict its result in writing. Then execute it and compare your prediction with the evidence. A useful explanation names the values at each step and the operation that transforms them. Console output is one form of evidence; a breakpoint lets you inspect the same state without adding permanent logging. Neither technique replaces reasoning about which instructions have actually executed.

Make a deliberate mistake, such as misspelling a variable, and inspect the resulting error. Identify the error type, the source location, and the first stack frame in your own code. Correct one cause at a time and rerun the smallest reproduction. This process develops a portable debugging habit: observation, hypothesis, isolated change, and confirmation. Keep a short notebook of mistaken predictions and their explanations.

Build the first useful slice

Your first program should have an observable result and a deliberately limited scope. A study-session estimator is enough: accept a number of lessons and minutes per lesson, compute a total, and present it clearly. Separate calculation from presentation even in this small example. A function that returns a number can later be used by a command-line interface, a browser page, or a test.

Write down assumptions before adding features: are fractional lessons allowed, can minutes be negative, and what should happen with missing input? You do not need an elaborate architecture to make these decisions explicit. Finish by explaining your program to an imaginary reviewer using concrete inputs. If the explanation requires guessing what a variable contains, improve the name or inspect the value before continuing.

Common pitfalls

  • Assuming every global function is part of the JavaScript language.
  • Making several unrelated edits before rerunning a failing example.

Retrieve what you learned

1. Which capability is supplied by a browser host?

  1. Array iteration
  2. Arithmetic operators
  3. The document object
  4. Function declarations
Answer and reasoning

C. The DOM document is a browser API; arrays, operators, and functions are language features.

2. What is the most useful next step after an unexpected result?

  1. Add a framework
  2. Reduce the example and inspect intermediate values
  3. Rewrite the entire file
  4. Ignore it if the page renders
Answer and reasoning

B. A small reproduction makes the causal chain visible and lets you test one hypothesis at a time.

Practice in your own editor

1. Runtime field notes

Run the same arithmetic function in a browser console and in Node.js. List three capabilities that differ between these environments.

Acceptance criteria
  • Both runs produce the same calculation.
  • Each difference names a host capability.

2. Prediction notebook

Predict five tiny expressions, run them, and explain every mismatch in one sentence.

Acceptance criteria
  • Predictions are recorded before execution.
  • Explanations identify an operation or value.

3. Session estimator

Build a function that calculates total study minutes and present its result separately.

Acceptance criteria
  • Calculation returns a number.
  • Zero lessons is handled.
  • At least three examples are documented.

Take it with you

  • A runtime combines the language with host APIs.
  • Predict, execute, inspect, and explain.
  • Small observable programs are powerful learning tools.
STAGE 1 / LESSON 2

Values, Types & Identity

Know what a variable contains and what an assignment copies.

Read: Ch. 2–3 · Lexical Structure; Types, Values, and Variables · Ch. 2; §§3.1–3.10
Suggested session: 55 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Distinguish primitive values from object references.
  • Choose explicit conversions for boundary inputs.
  • Explain const bindings, mutation, and equality.

Values are the starting point

JavaScript values have types even though a variable can hold different types over its lifetime. Common primitive types include number, string, boolean, undefined, null, bigint, and symbol. Objects include arrays and functions. A missing property typically evaluates to undefined; null is often an intentional marker selected by an API. These are different signals, so define what each means in your own program rather than treating every empty-looking value identically.

Input boundaries deserve special attention because form controls and command-line arguments commonly provide strings. The text "12" and the number 12 can participate in different operations. Convert deliberately, then validate the result with a check that matches your requirement. Number.isFinite rejects NaN and infinities without coercion. An empty string converts to zero with Number, which may be inappropriate for a required field.

const raw = "12";
const count = Number(raw);
console.log(Number.isFinite(count)); // true

Bindings are not containers that freeze objects

A variable binding associates a name with a value. const prevents reassignment of that binding; it does not make an object immutable. When two variables refer to the same object, changing a property through either name affects the same underlying object. By contrast, assigning a primitive gives another binding access to that immutable value, and later reassignment does not change the other binding.

Draw arrows when reasoning about identity. For const first = { score: 1 }; const second = first;, draw two names pointing to one object. For a spread copy, draw another outer object, but remember that nested objects are still shared. This visual distinction explains many surprising updates in application state. Decide whether a function may mutate its arguments and make that decision part of its contract.

const first = { score: 1 };
const second = first;
second.score += 1;
console.log(first.score); // 2

Conversions need a policy

Strict equality compares values without the coercion rules of loose equality. For objects, equality means identity, not matching contents. Two separately created arrays are different even when their elements look identical. Numeric calculations introduce another consideration: JavaScript numbers use floating-point representation, so some decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly. Compare calculated measurements using a tolerance appropriate to the problem instead of expecting every decimal result to be exact.

Keep lexical details clean while practicing these ideas: use descriptive identifiers, consistent punctuation, and strings whose quoting is easy to inspect. Separate raw input, converted values, and validated domain values with different names. Write a tiny table covering empty text, numeric text, invalid text, zero, and negative numbers. The table becomes a specification for your conversion policy and reveals whether the program accidentally accepts missing input.

Common pitfalls

  • Reading const as a promise that an object cannot change.
  • Using truthiness to validate a number when zero is a legitimate value.

Retrieve what you learned

1. What does const settings = { dark: false } prevent?

  1. Changing settings.dark
  2. Reassigning settings to another value
  3. Adding a property
  4. Reading settings
Answer and reasoning

B. const protects the binding; the referenced object remains mutable unless other measures are applied.

2. What is the result of [] === []?

  1. true
  2. false
  3. undefined
  4. A syntax error
Answer and reasoning

B. Each array literal creates a distinct object, and strict equality compares object identity.

Practice in your own editor

1. Identity sketches

Create examples of primitive assignment, object aliasing, and a shallow copy with nested data. Draw the reference graph for each.

Acceptance criteria
  • The nested copy example demonstrates sharing.
  • Predicted mutations match actual results.

2. Input boundary

Write parseLessonCount(raw) that accepts nonempty integer text representing a nonnegative count.

Acceptance criteria
  • Empty text is rejected.
  • Decimals and invalid text are rejected.
  • Zero is accepted.

3. Equality investigation

Compare pairs of primitives and objects, recording both their types and equality results.

Acceptance criteria
  • At least eight pairs are included.
  • Every object comparison explains identity.

Take it with you

  • const fixes a binding, not every property of an object.
  • Convert and validate at boundaries.
  • Object equality checks identity.
STAGE 1 / LESSON 3

Expressions That Tell the Truth

Make operators, defaults, and short-circuiting explicit.

Read: Ch. 4 · Expressions and Operators · §§4.1–4.13
Suggested session: 55 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Trace operator precedence and evaluation order.
  • Choose between logical OR and nullish defaults.
  • Write readable conditional and property-access expressions.

Expressions produce values and may do work

An expression evaluates to a value, but evaluation can also cause observable effects. A function call might write a log, mutate state, or start a request. Arithmetic, property access, comparisons, and assignments are all expressions with different rules. Operator precedence determines grouping; evaluation order determines when operands are evaluated. Parentheses make the intended grouping visible without requiring a reader to remember the entire precedence table.

Consider total = price + fee * quantity. Multiplication groups more tightly than addition, which may or may not match the business rule. Name intermediate values when an expression mixes several concepts. The goal is to expose the domain calculation: unit cost, subtotal, discount, and final amount. A few clear assignments often communicate more effectively than a compressed formula with several nested conditional operators.

const unitCost = price + fee;
const subtotal = unitCost * quantity;

Short-circuit operators return operands

The logical operators && and || select and return operand values; their results are not necessarily booleans. Evaluation may stop before the right operand runs. This allows compact checks but can hide side effects. The nullish coalescing operator ?? selects its fallback only for null or undefined, whereas || uses the broader category of falsy values. The distinction matters whenever zero, false, or an empty string is meaningful.

Build a small truth table for a setting such as playbackVolume. If zero means mute, volume || 50 changes a valid choice into a default. volume ?? 50 preserves it. Write the table before choosing an operator, and include absent values and valid edge values. When mixing nullish and logical operators, use explicit parentheses as required by the syntax and to make the policy immediately readable.

const savedVolume = 0;
console.log(savedVolume || 50); // 50
console.log(savedVolume ?? 50); // 0

Read safely without disguising invalid state

Optional chaining stops a property-access or call chain when the relevant receiver is null or undefined. It is useful when absence is expected, such as an optional profile. It does not validate the object, catch arbitrary exceptions, or guarantee that a present property has the right type. A required configuration value should usually be checked explicitly rather than silently replaced after every failed access.

Use a conditional expression for a simple choice between two values, and use statements when the branches perform several actions. Prefer boolean names such as isComplete when you need a boolean result. When reading unfamiliar code, annotate each expression with the value it returns and whether it can skip work. This discipline exposes accidental assignments in conditions, unexpected string concatenation, and defaults that erase legitimate values.

Common pitfalls

  • Assuming && and || always return true or false.
  • Using optional chaining everywhere and concealing a broken required invariant.

Retrieve what you learned

1. Which expression uses 10 only when value is null or undefined, while preserving a valid zero?

  1. value || 10
  2. value ?? 10
  3. Boolean(value) || 10
  4. value && 10
Answer and reasoning

B. Nullish coalescing falls back only for null and undefined, so it preserves zero.

2. What does false && expensiveOperation() do?

  1. Calls the function and returns false
  2. Skips the function and returns false
  3. Throws a TypeError
  4. Returns undefined
Answer and reasoning

B. Logical AND short-circuits when its left operand is falsy.

Practice in your own editor

1. Defaults matrix

Implement display-name and volume defaults with separate absence policies.

Acceptance criteria
  • A table covers null, undefined, empty string, zero, and false.
  • Each chosen operator is justified.

2. Expression refactor

Refactor a nested price calculation into named intermediate values.

Acceptance criteria
  • Outputs remain the same for three fixtures.
  • Each name describes a domain quantity.

3. Safe profile access

Read an optional avatar while rejecting a missing required user identifier.

Acceptance criteria
  • Optional absence has a fallback.
  • Invalid required state produces an explicit failure.

Take it with you

  • Expressions can return values and cause effects.
  • Choose defaults according to domain meaning.
  • Readable intermediate values are a debugging aid.
STAGE 1 / LESSON 4

Decisions & Defensive Control Flow

Turn vague requirements into complete branches.

Read: Ch. 5 · Statements · §§5.1–5.3; §§5.5.4, 5.5.6
Suggested session: 55 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Translate rules into mutually understood branches.
  • Use guard clauses and explicit failures.
  • Distinguish expected outcomes from exceptions.

A branch is a decision table in code

An if statement chooses which statements execute based on a condition. The challenge is usually not syntax but defining complete rules. Consider a course enrollment request: the course may be closed, the user may already be enrolled, or a seat may be available. Write these cases as a decision table, including their precedence. Otherwise the code may accidentally choose a convenient condition instead of the intended business outcome.

Use braces consistently so the scope of each branch is visible. Add boundary examples before implementing comparisons: exactly zero seats, exactly the minimum age, or exactly the deadline. These examples reveal whether the operator should be less than or less than or equal. When a condition becomes difficult to explain aloud, name it or extract a small predicate rather than adding another nested expression.

Guard clauses make the main path visible

A guard clause handles a special or invalid situation near the beginning of a function and exits early. This can keep the successful path at a consistent indentation level. It is especially effective at boundaries where raw input must satisfy a few clear requirements. The order of guards is part of the behavior: if several rules fail, the first guard determines which result or error the caller receives.

Do not confuse concise guards with incomplete validation. Decide whether a rejected request should return a structured result, return a sentinel value, or throw an exception. Expected user mistakes often work well as explicit results; violated programmer assumptions may justify exceptions. Whichever policy you choose, make the caller handle it consistently and ensure that no partial mutation happens before the validation finishes.

function enroll(seats) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(seats) || seats < 0) {
    throw new TypeError("seats must be a nonnegative integer");
  }
  if (seats === 0) return { ok: false, reason: "full" };
  return { ok: true, remaining: seats - 1 };
}

Choose branching structures for the domain

A switch statement is useful when one expression is compared against a fixed set of cases. Without a terminating statement, execution can continue into subsequent cases; this fallthrough should always be intentional and obvious. A lookup object may be clearer for a pure mapping, while if statements suit ranges and compound conditions. Select the structure that makes missing cases easy to notice during review.

Finish every decision function by looking for an unhandled situation. Unknown statuses, malformed values, and impossible combinations deserve explicit behavior. Test each branch using a representative example and test the boundaries between branches separately. This is more informative than repeatedly testing the common success path. Write the expected result before running the function so a surprising output cannot quietly become the new specification.

Common pitfalls

  • Validating after changing shared state.
  • Forgetting switch fallthrough or leaving unknown values undefined.

Retrieve what you learned

1. What should happen before mutating an enrollment record?

  1. Log the new record
  2. Validate all required preconditions
  3. Return a result
  4. Convert every value to a boolean
Answer and reasoning

B. Validation should precede mutation so rejected input cannot leave partially changed state.

2. Which test is most likely to expose an incorrect <= comparison?

  1. A random large value
  2. The exact boundary value
  3. Only the happy path
  4. An unrelated string
Answer and reasoning

B. Boundary tests distinguish inclusive from exclusive comparisons.

Practice in your own editor

1. Enrollment decision table

Specify and implement enrollment outcomes for closed, full, duplicate, and available courses.

Acceptance criteria
  • Rule precedence is written down.
  • Every row has a runnable example.

2. Guard-clause refactor

Flatten a deeply nested eligibility function using early returns.

Acceptance criteria
  • All original outcomes are preserved.
  • Invalid input causes no mutation.

3. Unknown status policy

Map lesson statuses to display labels and handle an unknown status intentionally.

Acceptance criteria
  • All known states are covered.
  • Unknown behavior is documented and tested.

Take it with you

  • Write the decision table before the branches.
  • Validate before effects.
  • Test the boundary, not only the center of each case.
STAGE 1 / LESSON 5

Loops, Collections & Invariants

Make repetition correct, bounded, and explainable.

Read: Ch. 5 · Statements · §§5.4–5.5
Suggested session: 55 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Choose a loop based on its stopping condition.
  • Explain loop invariants and off-by-one errors.
  • Use break and continue without hiding behavior.

Every loop needs a progress argument

A loop repeats work while a condition permits it. A useful explanation includes the initial state, the work performed, the state change, and the reason repetition eventually stops. For a counted loop, the index approaches an upper bound. For a search, the collection is exhausted or a match ends the loop. If you cannot identify a progress measure, the program may repeat forever on an unexpected input.

Start with the smallest collections: empty, one item, and two items. These cases make off-by-one mistakes visible. Prefer a half-open index range from zero up to but excluding length when indexing an array. Decide whether you need an index at all; for...of directly visits values of an iterable. Keep loop state close to the loop so the reader can see what controls termination.

An invariant explains why the result is trustworthy

A loop invariant is a statement that remains true before and after each iteration. When summing durations, the accumulator equals the sum of all items already processed. It begins at zero, each iteration adds exactly the next duration, and at termination every item has been processed. This style of reasoning makes correctness concrete and exposes duplicate processing, skipped values, and accidental resets inside a loop.

Write an invariant in a comment for your first few algorithms. Then trace one input in a table with columns for the index, current value, and accumulator. Include a negative value or another edge case if the contract permits it. The purpose is to connect the implementation to a claim you can verify, rather than assuming that a plausible-looking loop must be correct.

let total = 0;
for (const minutes of [15, 25, 10]) {
  // Before each step, total covers the preceding values.
  total += minutes;
}
console.log(total); // 50

Early exits are part of the contract

break stops the nearest enclosing loop, while continue skips the remaining work in the current iteration. Both can express useful rules, such as finding the first matching lesson or ignoring a canceled session. They can also obscure the relationship between counters and processed records. Decide whether your result describes all input, only valid input, or the prefix before an early exit, and name it accordingly.

Do not use for...in as a substitute for value iteration over arrays; it enumerates property keys and brings a different set of semantics. Avoid modifying a collection while traversing it unless you have reasoned about how the iteration sees changes. For an initial implementation, accumulate a new collection and keep the source stable. Make any intentional mutation visible in the function name or documentation.

Common pitfalls

  • Using an inclusive upper bound with a zero-based array index.
  • Updating a progress counter only on some paths through the loop.

Retrieve what you learned

1. Which indexed loop covers an array without reading past its end?

  1. i <= items.length
  2. i < items.length
  3. i > items.length
  4. i === items.length
Answer and reasoning

B. Valid indexes range from zero to length minus one, so the upper bound is exclusive.

2. What does continue do?

  1. Ends the function
  2. Ends all enclosing loops
  3. Skips to the next iteration of the nearest loop
  4. Restarts the program
Answer and reasoning

C. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and proceeds according to the loop mechanics.

Practice in your own editor

1. Trace a total

Implement a duration sum and trace empty, single-item, and mixed-duration inputs.

Acceptance criteria
  • An invariant is written.
  • Each item contributes exactly once.

2. First unfinished lesson

Find the first unfinished lesson without scanning remaining items after a match.

Acceptance criteria
  • Empty and fully completed collections return a documented result.
  • The first matching item is selected.

3. Streak calculator

Calculate the longest run of true values representing successful study days.

Acceptance criteria
  • Empty input returns zero.
  • Runs at the beginning and end are handled.
  • The invariant explains both counters.

Take it with you

  • A loop needs a visible stopping condition.
  • Invariants connect each iteration to the final claim.
  • Empty and single-item inputs are essential examples.
STAGE 1 / LESSON 6

Scope, Errors & Small Programs

Combine the fundamentals into a dependable command.

Read: Ch. 3 & 5 · Variables and Statements · §3.10; §§5.5.6–5.5.7, 5.7
Suggested session: 75 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Explain lexical scope and temporal dead zones.
  • Propagate errors with useful context.
  • Deliver a small program with explicit input and output contracts.

Scope determines where a binding can be used

Lexical scope is determined by the structure of source code. A binding declared inside a block with let or const is available within that block and its nested scopes, subject to initialization rules. A same-named inner binding shadows an outer one. This can be useful, but unnecessary shadowing makes debugging harder because a familiar name may refer to a different value at a different location.

Declarations with let and const have a temporal dead zone before initialization. Access during that interval throws rather than returning undefined. Avoid relying on declaration quirks: declare values near their first meaningful use, prefer narrow scopes, and use distinct names when they represent different concepts. These habits reduce the amount of program state you must mentally track while reviewing a function or investigating a failure.

const goal = 4;
{
  const completed = 2;
  console.log(goal - completed);
}
// completed is not accessible here.

Errors should preserve the useful story

Throwing an error transfers control until an appropriate catch handler is found. Use an Error object so the failure carries a name, message, and stack trace. A catch block should recover, translate the failure at a boundary, or add useful context before rethrowing. Catching everything and returning an arbitrary default can turn a clear failure into corrupt output that appears successful to its caller.

A finally block runs when leaving the try statement, including many abrupt exits, and is useful for cleanup. Avoid returning from finally because that return can replace an earlier result or exception. At the application boundary, present a concise message and retain diagnostic details for debugging. Within calculation functions, keep failures precise enough that a caller can distinguish invalid input from a defect in the implementation.

Deliver a complete small slice

Build a study-plan calculator that accepts lesson counts and time estimates, computes a schedule, and returns a structured result. Keep parsing, validation, calculation, and display as separate responsibilities. This separation is useful even before modules: each part can be called with a small example. Define whether the program rounds up sessions, permits zero available minutes, and treats an empty plan as valid input.

Use a short acceptance checklist: normal inputs produce expected totals, boundary inputs have specified behavior, invalid inputs fail clearly, and no hidden global state changes the result. Add a README-style explanation in your own notes with one successful example and one rejected example. Review the program by tracing a value from raw input to final output, identifying the contract at every transition. This is your first miniature engineering review.

Common pitfalls

  • Using a catch block to hide errors without a recovery policy.
  • Returning from finally and accidentally overriding a thrown error.

Retrieve what you learned

1. What happens when a let binding is read before initialization in its scope?

  1. It always returns undefined
  2. It throws a ReferenceError
  3. It reads the outer value automatically
  4. It becomes null
Answer and reasoning

B. The binding exists but is in its temporal dead zone until initialization.

2. Where should a friendly user-facing error usually be created?

  1. At the application boundary
  2. Inside every arithmetic expression
  3. In a finally return
  4. Only in comments
Answer and reasoning

A. The boundary can translate internal failures into an appropriate presentation while preserving diagnostic context.

Practice in your own editor

1. Scope detective

Create three examples involving block scope, shadowing, and access before initialization.

Acceptance criteria
  • Each prediction identifies the binding involved.
  • Failures name the expected error type.

2. Error path audit

Add explicit validation and boundary error reporting to your session estimator.

Acceptance criteria
  • Invalid input is distinguishable from a valid zero result.
  • The original error is not silently discarded.

3. Stage project: study-plan calculator

Deliver a planner with parsing, validation, totals, and a concise usage guide.

Acceptance criteria
  • Five acceptance cases pass.
  • No calculation depends on a mutable global.
  • A peer could run it using your instructions.

Take it with you

  • Lexical structure determines scope.
  • Handle errors where you can make a useful decision.
  • A complete small program includes its failure behavior.
STAGE 2 / LESSON 7

Objects as Models

Give records clear meaning and predictable update rules.

Read: Ch. 6 · Objects · §§6.1–6.10
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Model records using intentional property names.
  • Distinguish property absence from an undefined value.
  • Perform shallow updates without misunderstanding nested references.

A record is a set of domain decisions

An object groups properties under a single identity. Before writing a literal, decide what the record represents and which properties are required. A lesson record might contain id, title, durationMinutes, and status. Names encode units and meaning; durationMinutes prevents confusion that a generic duration invites. A stable identifier lets other records refer to a lesson without depending on a title that may change during editing.

Property keys are strings or symbols, and bracket notation evaluates an expression to choose a key. Dot notation is convenient for a known identifier-like name. When a key comes from input, validate it against the operation you intend to support. A general-purpose object updater that accepts every possible property is harder to reason about than a small operation such as renameLesson or completeLesson.

const lesson = { id: "L1", title: "Values", durationMinutes: 45 };
const field = "title";
console.log(lesson[field]);

Presence and value are different questions

Reading a missing property usually returns undefined, but an existing property can also hold undefined. The in operator checks whether a property exists anywhere along the prototype chain. Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(record, key) checks an own property and works even when the record has a conflicting property name. Choose the question that matches the contract rather than treating all these checks as interchangeable.

Enumeration also has specific rules. Object.keys returns enumerable own string keys; it does not include every possible property. Object.entries is useful when processing a record as pairs. Keep data records simple while learning: avoid mixing arbitrary inherited behavior into objects that are primarily serialized data. Make optional properties intentional and document whether omission, undefined, or null represents the absence your application needs.

Updates need an ownership policy

Object spread creates a new outer object and copies enumerable own properties. It does not recursively clone every referenced object. If a record contains a nested progress object, both copies may still share it. An immutable nested update must copy each object along the changed path, or use a different data layout that reduces nesting. The right choice depends on the size and complexity of the model.

Write operations that return a new record when callers should retain the previous snapshot. Alternatively, explicitly allow mutation when one component owns the record exclusively. What causes trouble is an undocumented mixture of both policies. Check updates with assertions about both values and identity: the changed record should contain the new value, the previous record should remain correct, and intentionally unchanged branches may still share references.

Common pitfalls

  • Confusing property absence with a present undefined value.
  • Assuming object spread recursively copies nested records.

Retrieve what you learned

1. What does {...record} create?

  1. A recursive deep clone
  2. A shallow copy of enumerable own properties
  3. The same object
  4. A frozen object
Answer and reasoning

B. Spread copies the outer properties; nested references are still shared.

2. Which check includes inherited properties?

  1. Object.keys(obj)
  2. "name" in obj
  3. JSON.stringify(obj)
  4. obj === "name"
Answer and reasoning

B. The in operator searches the prototype chain as well as own properties.

Practice in your own editor

1. Lesson schema

Design a lesson record and document every property, type, and absence rule.

Acceptance criteria
  • Units appear in relevant names.
  • Identity is independent of title.

2. Safe rename

Implement renameLesson(record, title) without changing the original record.

Acceptance criteria
  • The title is validated.
  • The returned object has a different identity.

3. Nested progress update

Update a nested completion flag while preserving the original snapshot.

Acceptance criteria
  • Changed ancestors are copied.
  • Unchanged data remains correct.

Take it with you

  • Model domain meaning before syntax.
  • Presence and value require different checks.
  • Copy depth follows the update path.
STAGE 2 / LESSON 8

Arrays as Data Pipelines

Express selection, transformation, and aggregation clearly.

Read: Ch. 7 · Arrays · §§7.1–7.10
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Choose map, filter, find, and reduce by intent.
  • Control mutation when sorting or editing arrays.
  • Handle empty and sparse collections deliberately.

Choose an operation that explains the result

An array is an ordered collection whose elements are accessed by numeric indexes. A pipeline becomes readable when each operation describes a distinct transformation. filter selects elements, map produces one output for each visited element, find returns the first match, and reduce accumulates a result. Begin by writing the desired input and output shapes. Then choose operations that communicate how one shape becomes the other.

Do not use map simply to perform side effects while discarding its returned array. A loop or forEach states that intention more clearly. A long pipeline can also become obscure when callbacks mix filtering, mutation, and logging. Name meaningful intermediate collections during development. Clear stages make it easier to inspect an unexpected result and isolate whether selection, conversion, or aggregation introduced the error.

const lessons = [{ minutes: 20, done: true }, { minutes: 35, done: false }];
const remainingMinutes = lessons
  .filter(lesson => !lesson.done)
  .reduce((total, lesson) => total + lesson.minutes, 0);

Order and mutation are part of the contract

Methods such as sort, reverse, splice, push, and pop mutate their receiver. Other methods return a new array. If callers retain earlier snapshots, copy before using a mutating operation. A numeric sort requires a comparator such as (a, b) => a - b; the default sort compares string representations. For records, define a primary key and a tie-breaking rule when deterministic ordering matters.

An array copy still shares object elements. Sorting a copied array preserves the source order, but mutating an element in the copy may affect the source record. Test these as separate concerns: array identity, element identity, order, and property values. The distinction becomes central when a user interface stores snapshots or a function promises to leave its input unchanged for later comparison.

Empty input is a real input

An empty collection should have an explicit result. Summing zero durations naturally gives zero, so provide an initial accumulator to reduce. Finding a missing record returns undefined. Computing an average requires an additional policy because dividing an empty total by zero does not produce a meaningful domain value. Do not let an incidental arithmetic result decide how the product represents missing information.

Sparse arrays contain missing indexes, which differ from indexes explicitly holding undefined. Different operations can observe holes differently, making sparse arrays a poor default for application collections. Build dense arrays by appending actual records or mapping well-defined sources. For every pipeline, include empty input, one element, duplicates, and invalid records in your review. Explain whether invalid records are rejected or excluded, and avoid silently changing that policy between steps.

Common pitfalls

  • Sorting numbers without a comparator.
  • Calling reduce without an initial value when the collection may be empty.

Retrieve what you learned

1. Which operation returns the first matching value?

  1. map
  2. find
  3. filter
  4. sort
Answer and reasoning

B. find returns one matching element or undefined; filter returns an array.

2. How can you sort numeric values without changing the source order?

  1. values.sort()
  2. [...values].sort((a,b) => a-b)
  3. values.reverse()
  4. values.push(0)
Answer and reasoning

B. The spread makes a new outer array and the comparator performs numeric ordering.

Practice in your own editor

1. Learning dashboard

Compute unfinished titles, total remaining minutes, and the next unfinished lesson.

Acceptance criteria
  • Empty input has defined results.
  • Input records are not mutated.

2. Stable priority list

Sort lessons by priority and then title while preserving the source order.

Acceptance criteria
  • A numeric comparator is used for priority.
  • Ties have a documented rule.

3. Pipeline review

Write both a loop and a method pipeline for grouping total minutes by stage.

Acceptance criteria
  • Both implementations agree on four fixtures.
  • You explain which version is clearer.

Take it with you

  • Let each collection operation state an intention.
  • Array copying does not clone every element.
  • Specify empty-input behavior.
STAGE 2 / LESSON 9

Functions & API Contracts

Design callable units that are easy to trust and test.

Read: Ch. 8 · Functions · §§8.1–8.3
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Write explicit parameter and return-value contracts.
  • Separate pure calculations from observable effects.
  • Choose function forms for clarity and behavior.

A function is a promise to its caller

A function contract states accepted inputs, the returned value, possible failures, and observable effects. For calculateCompletion(completed, total), decide whether total may be zero, whether fractions are allowed, and whether completed may exceed total. Without these rules, even a two-line function is ambiguous. A good name narrows the promise, and a concise comment records details that cannot be inferred from the name alone.

Implement the smallest function that fulfills one promise. If a function parses input, updates storage, renders a message, and calculates a percentage, failures become difficult to isolate. Split responsibilities at useful boundaries, not at arbitrary line counts. A slightly longer function with one coherent purpose is often easier to understand than several tiny helpers whose names do not explain why they exist.

Pure functions are convenient test surfaces

A pure calculation depends only on its inputs and produces no externally visible mutation. Calling it with equivalent inputs yields equivalent results, which makes examples easy to reproduce. Effects such as reading the current clock, writing storage, and modifying the DOM are still necessary, but can sit outside the calculation. Pass needed environmental values as arguments so the core decision remains deterministic.

For a deadline checker, supply now rather than calling Date.now deep inside the rule. For a recommendation function, pass the lessons instead of reading a global array. These changes make the hidden dependencies visible. Test both the returned value and the promise that input objects remain unchanged. Purity is a design tool, not a requirement for every function; effectful functions should simply make their responsibilities explicit.

function remainingMinutes(planned, completed) {
  if (completed > planned) throw new RangeError("completed exceeds planned");
  return planned - completed;
}

Function forms carry different semantics

Function declarations, function expressions, and arrow functions can all describe callable behavior, but they are not interchangeable in every situation. Declarations have useful initialization behavior within their scope. Arrow functions use lexical this and do not provide their own arguments object. A concise arrow body returns its expression; a block body requires an explicit return when a value is intended.

Choose a consistent form for the role, and optimize for the next reader. A named function improves stack traces and explains a substantial operation; a short arrow works well as a local transformation callback. Watch for implicit undefined when a branch forgets to return. Build a contract table containing normal cases, boundary cases, and rejected cases, then use it to assess every path through the implementation.

Common pitfalls

  • Letting a calculation read hidden global state.
  • Forgetting return inside an arrow function with a block body.

Retrieve what you learned

1. What makes a calculation easier to reproduce?

  1. Reading the current time internally
  2. Receiving all relevant values as arguments
  3. Mutating a shared cache
  4. Catching every error
Answer and reasoning

B. Explicit inputs make the dependencies visible and the result reproducible.

2. What does x => { x * 2; } return?

  1. Twice x
  2. undefined
  3. null
  4. A syntax error
Answer and reasoning

B. A block-bodied arrow needs an explicit return statement.

Practice in your own editor

1. Completion contract

Specify and implement a completion percentage function.

Acceptance criteria
  • Zero-total behavior is explicit.
  • Invalid counts are rejected.

2. Extract the core

Refactor a function that logs a deadline result into a pure decision and a presentation step.

Acceptance criteria
  • The current time is an argument.
  • The decision can run without a console.

3. Return-path audit

Review five short functions and identify missing or inconsistent returns.

Acceptance criteria
  • Every path matches the documented return shape.
  • Examples exercise each branch.

Take it with you

  • Contracts include effects and failures.
  • Explicit inputs make calculations reproducible.
  • A function form has semantics beyond its appearance.
STAGE 2 / LESSON 10

Closures & Higher-Order Functions

Use captured state and behavior as deliberate building blocks.

Read: Ch. 8 · Functions · §§8.4–8.6, 8.8
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Explain what a closure captures.
  • Build a stateful function factory with controlled ownership.
  • Use higher-order functions to compose behavior.

Functions retain access to lexical bindings

A closure combines a function with access to the lexical environment where it was created. The function can continue using those bindings after the outer call has returned. It captures access to bindings, not a frozen snapshot of every value. If a captured binding changes, a later call observes the current value. This explains both useful private state and confusing behavior in callbacks created around shared mutable variables.

Trace a factory by drawing one environment for each invocation. Two calls to makeCounter create independent count bindings, while two references to the same returned function share one environment. Block-scoped let in a loop gives callbacks the expected per-iteration binding in common patterns. Practice predicting these relationships before executing the code; the model is more durable than memorizing a closure definition.

function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;
  return () => ++count;
}
const first = makeCounter();
const second = makeCounter();
console.log(first(), first(), second()); // 1 2 1

Private state still needs a clear contract

A function factory can expose a small API while keeping implementation state out of direct reach. A study timer might expose start, pause, and elapsed functions that share one private state. The absence of public properties does not automatically make the design correct: you still need valid transitions, clear ownership, and behavior for repeated calls. Closure-based encapsulation is useful when it reduces the number of states callers can create.

Be careful about retaining large objects through long-lived closures. A registered callback may keep its environment reachable even after a screen disappears. Define a cleanup path for subscriptions and timers when the surrounding component owns them. During testing, create fresh factories for independent cases so captured state does not leak between tests and make outcomes depend on execution order.

Behavior can be passed like other data

A higher-order function accepts functions, returns functions, or both. Array methods are familiar examples, but you can also build reusable policies such as withLogging, once, or a predicate combiner. Keep the wrapped function contract intact: preserve argument handling, returned values, and thrown errors unless the wrapper explicitly promises to change them. Otherwise a useful-looking abstraction can subtly break the caller.

Start with a small composition exercise: trim a string, normalize case, and validate the result using separate functions. Name intermediate behavior when it improves readability. Avoid building a generic functional framework before a real repetition appears. The purpose of higher-order functions is to express reusable behavior clearly, and the best abstraction is usually the smallest one that removes an actual duplication in your program.

Common pitfalls

  • Thinking a closure captures an immutable copy of a variable.
  • Sharing one factory instance across tests that should be independent.

Retrieve what you learned

1. Two independent calls to makeCounter usually create what?

  1. One shared count binding
  2. Two separate lexical environments
  3. No retained state
  4. A global variable
Answer and reasoning

B. Each invocation creates its own environment, retained by its returned closure.

2. A wrapper that calls a function but omits return changes what?

  1. Only formatting
  2. The return-value contract
  3. The function name only
  4. Nothing observable
Answer and reasoning

B. Callers receive undefined instead of the wrapped function result.

Practice in your own editor

1. Private attempt tracker

Create a factory with recordAttempt and getAttempts operations.

Acceptance criteria
  • Instances are independent.
  • Callers cannot mutate internal history directly.

2. Once wrapper

Implement once(fn) and define whether failures count as an invocation.

Acceptance criteria
  • Return values are preserved.
  • Failure policy is documented.

3. Predicate toolkit

Combine small predicates to select lessons matching duration and completion criteria.

Acceptance criteria
  • Predicates are independently testable.
  • Composition does not mutate records.

Take it with you

  • Closures retain access to bindings.
  • Each factory call can own independent state.
  • Wrappers must preserve or explicitly change contracts.
STAGE 2 / LESSON 11

Parameters, Context & Composition

Make invocation behavior explicit at every call site.

Read: Ch. 8 · Functions · §§8.2–8.3, 8.7–8.8
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Use defaults, rest parameters, and destructuring intentionally.
  • Explain this according to invocation style.
  • Compose functions without hiding dependencies.

Parameters are the front door of an API

Default parameters apply when an argument is omitted or explicitly undefined, not when it is null. Rest parameters collect remaining arguments into an actual array. Destructuring can make an options object readable and reduce positional ambiguity. For example, schedule({ minutes, breakMinutes = 5 }) communicates more clearly than schedule(25, 5, true, false), especially when several values share the same primitive type.

Defaults should encode a product decision rather than conceal required input. If a course identifier is mandatory, a fallback identifier may route work incorrectly instead of helping. Validate options after applying legitimate defaults, and decide how unknown properties are handled. A small options object is often enough; avoid allowing every internal detail to become a public option because each option creates a contract you must maintain.

The call site determines ordinary this

For an ordinary function, this depends on how it is called. A method invocation such as timer.start() supplies the receiver as this. Extracting const start = timer.start and calling start() loses that receiver. In strict mode, a plain function call has undefined this. Arrow functions behave differently: they inherit this from the surrounding lexical environment instead of receiving it from a method call.

Use bind when you intentionally need a function permanently associated with a receiver, or use a small closure that makes the intended call explicit. Do not automatically bind every method; first ask whether the operation needs this at all. Passing data as a parameter can be clearer for reusable calculations. Predict the receiver at the call site before interpreting a method body that reads properties through this.

const timer = { minutes: 25, read() { return this.minutes; } };
const readTimer = () => timer.read();
console.log(readTimer()); // 25

Composition makes dependencies visible

Composition builds larger behavior by combining smaller functions with compatible contracts. A parsing function can produce a validated count, which a planner turns into a schedule, which a formatter turns into text. The boundaries work when each output shape matches the next input shape. If each step catches failures differently or mutates shared state, a neat pipeline can hide a difficult execution model.

Document the intermediate values for one complete example. Then inject a failure at each boundary and trace who handles it. This reveals whether errors are duplicated, swallowed, or translated too early. Prefer a clear sequence of named steps to an elaborate compose utility until repetition justifies the abstraction. Review both the successful data path and the failed path as first-class parts of the resulting API.

Common pitfalls

  • Expecting a default parameter to replace null.
  • Passing an extracted method as a callback and losing its receiver.

Retrieve what you learned

1. When does a default parameter apply?

  1. For every falsy value
  2. For undefined or an omitted argument
  3. Only for null
  4. Only for zero
Answer and reasoning

B. Default parameters activate for undefined, including omitted arguments.

2. Why can const fn = obj.method; fn() fail?

  1. Functions cannot be assigned
  2. The call no longer supplies obj as the receiver
  3. The method is deleted
  4. const freezes the function
Answer and reasoning

B. Ordinary this depends on the invocation, so extracting a method loses its object receiver.

Practice in your own editor

1. Options API

Refactor a scheduling function from positional arguments to a documented options object.

Acceptance criteria
  • Required fields remain required.
  • Defaults distinguish undefined from null.

2. Lost receiver lab

Create and repair an extracted-method callback using a closure and bind.

Acceptance criteria
  • You explain both repairs.
  • A test demonstrates the original failure.

3. Import pipeline

Compose text parsing, validation, planning, and formatting functions.

Acceptance criteria
  • Every intermediate shape is documented.
  • Each failure reaches one clear boundary.

Take it with you

  • Defaults apply to undefined.
  • Ordinary this follows the call site.
  • Composition depends on compatible contracts.
STAGE 2 / LESSON 12

Data Modeling Studio

Build a small learning planner with a dependable core.

Read: Ch. 6–8 · Objects, Arrays, and Functions · Integration studio · Chapters 6–8
Suggested session: 90 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Design a normalized model for lessons and progress.
  • Implement domain operations with explicit invariants.
  • Evaluate the core using fixtures and a review rubric.

Start with the questions the model must answer

A useful model supports the operations your application needs. A learning planner must list lessons, record completion, estimate remaining time, and choose the next session. Separate lesson definitions from learner progress: a title belongs to the curriculum, while completedAt belongs to one learner. Give records stable identifiers and use those identifiers for relationships. This avoids duplicating mutable titles or entire lesson objects inside every progress entry.

Write three realistic fixtures before implementing behavior: a new learner, a learner halfway through a stage, and a learner who has completed everything. Add an intentionally malformed fixture to exercise validation. Inspect whether the model answers each required question without redundant sources of truth. Storing both completedCount and a completion map, for example, creates an obligation to keep them synchronized after every update.

Build operations around invariants

An invariant is a rule the model must preserve after every public operation. A completed lesson must exist in the curriculum; duration must be finite and nonnegative; progress for one learner must not mutate another learner. Implement focused operations such as completeLesson, reopenLesson, and planSession. Let each operation validate its inputs before creating a new state or changing owned state according to your chosen policy.

Define selection behavior precisely. A session planner may choose unfinished lessons in curriculum order until its time budget is exhausted. Decide whether an oversized first lesson is skipped, included with a warning, or causes an empty plan. Different policies are defensible, but accidental behavior is not. Use examples that distinguish the policies, including an exact budget fit and a remaining lesson longer than the entire budget.

const progress = { completedIds: ["L1"] };
const completed = new Set(progress.completedIds);
const unfinished = lessons.filter(lesson => !completed.has(lesson.id));

Review the result like a small product

Keep the domain core independent of display and storage so you can exercise it with fixtures. A thin presentation function can produce a readable report containing total lessons, completed lessons, remaining minutes, and the next session. Include an explanation when no session can be planned. This converts internal decisions into behavior that a user can understand and gives you a concrete artifact to review.

Use a weighted rubric: correctness forty percent, clear contracts twenty-five percent, meaningful examples twenty percent, and readable naming fifteen percent. A submission is ready when all invariants hold across the fixtures and another person can explain the update policy from the public functions. Record one design tradeoff and one possible future extension. Avoid adding that extension until the present requirements are complete and the existing model remains easy to inspect.

Common pitfalls

  • Duplicating derived totals and forgetting to synchronize them.
  • Leaving session-budget policy to incidental loop behavior.

Retrieve what you learned

1. Where should completedAt usually live?

  1. On the shared lesson definition
  2. In learner-specific progress
  3. In a function name
  4. Only in a console log
Answer and reasoning

B. Completion is learner-specific state, while lesson definitions describe shared curriculum.

2. Which example distinguishes budget boundary behavior?

  1. Only a large budget
  2. A lesson whose duration exactly equals the budget
  3. An unrelated title
  4. A random identifier
Answer and reasoning

B. An exact fit exposes whether the planner handles inclusive budget boundaries correctly.

Practice in your own editor

1. Model proposal

Write the lesson, learner-progress, and session shapes plus their invariants.

Acceptance criteria
  • Shared definitions are separate from learner state.
  • Derived fields have an explicit policy.

2. Domain implementation

Implement completion, reopening, summaries, and session planning.

Acceptance criteria
  • Unknown lesson IDs are rejected.
  • Exact-budget and oversized-lesson cases are covered.

3. Stage review

Deliver the planner with three realistic fixtures, a malformed fixture, and a short design note.

Acceptance criteria
  • The weighted rubric is scored honestly.
  • Every public function has an example.
  • A future extension is described without speculative code.

Take it with you

  • Model the questions your product must answer.
  • Preserve invariants through every operation.
  • A studio includes evidence and a design explanation.
STAGE 3 / LESSON 13

Prototypes & the Object Model

Understand the lookup mechanism behind objects and methods.

Read: Ch. 9 · Classes · §§9.1–9.2; review §6.3
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Trace property lookup through a prototype chain.
  • Separate inherited behavior from instance data.
  • Explain constructor and prototype relationships.

Lookup follows a chain

When an object lacks an own property, JavaScript searches its prototype chain until a property is found or the chain ends at null. A prototype is another object, so the same mechanism can repeat through several levels. This shares behavior without copying every method into every instance. A missing property usually produces undefined after the search is exhausted.

Draw an instance with an own title and an inherited describe method. Label where each property lives and where each read finds it. Distinguish the internal prototype relationship from a function's ordinary property named prototype. Object.getPrototypeOf reveals the former. Understanding that distinction prevents the common mistake of treating all properties with similar names as the same mechanism.

Reads and writes have different rules

A read can find inherited data, while ordinary assignment often creates an own property that shadows inherited data. Accessors and nonwritable properties introduce additional rules, so inspect descriptors when behavior is surprising. Deleting an own property can reveal an inherited property again. It does not necessarily make every future read of that name return undefined.

Mutable instance data should not accidentally live on a shared prototype. If two learners inherit one history array, pushing through either learner changes the same array. Give each learner an independent array. Shared methods are appropriate because they obtain working state from their receiver. Test both the values and reference identities when diagnosing shared-state bugs.

const methods = { describe() { return this.title; } };
const lesson = Object.create(methods);
lesson.title = "Prototypes";
console.log(lesson.describe());

Construction connects identity and behavior

Calling a suitable function with new creates an object, connects its prototype, invokes the constructor with the new receiver, and normally returns that object. Class syntax organizes construction and methods around this prototype-based model. Instances remain ordinary objects with identity and properties; they are not a separate value system disconnected from the rest of JavaScript.

Use prototype inspection for learning and debugging, but avoid changing prototype relationships casually during normal execution. Stable relationships are easier to explain and maintain. Before introducing a class, decide whether the model needs coordinated behavior around an identity or whether a plain record and functions already describe the domain clearly. Shared behavior is a capability, not a requirement for every object. Compare an own-property check with the in operator so your diagram distinguishes storage location from successful lookup through inheritance.

Common pitfalls

  • Putting per-instance mutable arrays on a shared prototype.
  • Confusing an internal prototype with a property named prototype.

Retrieve what you learned

1. Where should independent learner history live?

  1. On a shared prototype array
  2. On each instance
  3. On Object.prototype
  4. In one global array
Answer and reasoning

B. Instance-specific state needs independent ownership.

2. Deleting an own property can reveal what?

  1. An inherited property
  2. A new global
  3. A copied constructor
  4. A syntax error
Answer and reasoning

A. The next read searches the prototype chain.

Practice in your own editor

1. Lookup diagram

Diagram five reads through a two-level prototype chain.

Acceptance criteria
  • Own and inherited locations are labeled.
  • A missing read reaches null.

2. Shared-state repair

Reproduce and repair a shared prototype-array bug.

Acceptance criteria
  • Two instances expose the bug.
  • The repair gives independent histories.

3. Construction comparison

Build equivalent objects with Object.create and a constructor.

Acceptance criteria
  • Prototype relationships are inspected.
  • Shared methods read instance data.

Take it with you

  • Lookup follows a chain.
  • Shared behavior differs from shared mutable data.
  • Classes use the object model.
STAGE 3 / LESSON 14

Classes with Clear Invariants

Design instances whose valid states are easy to understand.

Read: Ch. 9 · Classes · §§9.3–9.4
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Establish invariants during construction.
  • Distinguish static operations from instance methods.
  • Test valid transitions and rejected operations.

Construction establishes valid state

A class groups construction and related behavior under one name. Its constructor should finish with an instance that satisfies the domain rules. A study session might require a positive duration and begin idle. Validate inputs before making the instance available to other code. Avoid implicit network requests or timers during construction when explicit startup would make ownership clearer.

List the fields and the relationships between them. If startedAt is meaningful only while running, every operation must preserve that relationship. Alternatively, choose a representation with fewer impossible combinations. A class earns its place when it coordinates behavior around identity or protects meaningful invariants. Merely wrapping a record in constructor syntax does not automatically improve its design.

Methods express transitions

Methods such as start, pause, and complete describe domain transitions more clearly than unrestricted setters for each field. Decide what repeated calls mean: starting an already running session could return its current state or reject the operation. Either policy can work, but callers need a predictable contract. Validate a transition before changing several related fields.

Static methods belong to the class object and can provide named construction helpers such as fromRecord. Getters can expose computed values without storing redundant state. Keep apparently simple reads free of surprising expensive effects. A public surface should let callers distinguish inspection from change and understand which operations can fail before they use the object in a larger workflow.

class Session {
  constructor(minutes) {
    if (!Number.isFinite(minutes) || minutes <= 0) throw new RangeError("Invalid duration");
    this.minutes = minutes;
    this.state = "idle";
  }
  start() {
    if (this.state !== "idle") throw new Error("Invalid transition");
    this.state = "running";
  }
}

Encapsulation supports change

Encapsulation lets callers rely on a stable interface while internal representation evolves. Naming conventions communicate intent; closures and language features can enforce parts of the boundary. The central question is whether callers can bypass the operations that preserve invariants. If they can create impossible states through public fields, additional validation or a narrower interface is necessary.

Test the class through construction, queries, and transitions. Include malformed constructor inputs and invalid transition sequences. Verify failures leave state unchanged. Tests that rely on every private implementation detail make later improvements difficult, so prefer observable behavior. A strong interface lets you replace a stored derived value with a calculation while keeping callers and their meaningful tests correct. Review each public method against a transition table, including repeated calls and failures, before considering the interface complete.

Common pitfalls

  • Exposing setters that bypass domain invariants.
  • Starting unmanaged resources during construction.

Retrieve what you learned

1. What should successful construction guarantee?

  1. Every future call succeeds
  2. The initial state is valid
  3. All fields are public
  4. No mutation is possible
Answer and reasoning

B. Construction establishes invariants that methods must preserve.

2. Which operation fits a static method?

  1. Pause this session
  2. Read this elapsed value
  3. Construct from a validated record
  4. Increment this counter
Answer and reasoning

C. A construction helper operates before a particular instance exists.

Practice in your own editor

1. Session machine

Implement idle, running, paused, and completed transitions.

Acceptance criteria
  • Allowed transitions are listed.
  • Rejected transitions preserve state.

2. Record factory

Create validated instances from serialized records.

Acceptance criteria
  • Malformed data is rejected.
  • Valid records produce usable instances.

3. Boundary review

Compare unrestricted fields with an invariant-preserving interface.

Acceptance criteria
  • A violation is demonstrated.
  • The chosen boundary is justified.

Take it with you

  • Constructors establish invariants.
  • Methods preserve valid transitions.
  • Behavioral tests support representation changes.
STAGE 3 / LESSON 15

Inheritance & Composition

Choose relationships that preserve meaning under change.

Read: Ch. 9 · Classes · §9.5 · Subclasses and delegation
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Evaluate subtype behavior against a base contract.
  • Compose independent policies using collaborators.
  • Document architecture tradeoffs with concrete changes.

Inheritance is a behavioral commitment

A subclass inherits behavior and may override it. The important question is whether a caller expecting the base abstraction can use the subclass without surprising changes. Matching method names is insufficient. Accepted inputs, results, failures, and effects all contribute to the contract. A supposedly general collection that unexpectedly rejects ordinary additions may violate its caller's reasonable expectations.

Write one consumer of the base interface and run it against each proposed subtype. If the consumer needs repeated subtype checks, inspect the hierarchy. Shared fields alone rarely justify inheritance. In a derived constructor, super must initialize the base instance before this is used. Keep initialization responsibilities explicit so state cannot be partially established through an unclear chain of constructor assumptions.

Composition separates independent policies

Composition gives an object collaborators instead of encoding every variation in ancestry. A planner can receive a selection strategy and a storage adapter. Changing selection then does not require a new storage subclass, and changing storage does not duplicate selection logic. This matters when two independent choices would otherwise create a growing number of combined subclasses.

Keep collaborator interfaces narrow and behavioral. A selection strategy can simply accept lessons and a budget and return a plan. Specify mutation and failure rules as well as parameter names. Inject a fake collaborator to control outcomes in tests. Avoid creating interfaces for imaginary future changes; extract the boundary when it clarifies a present responsibility or a plausible, concrete variation.

function createPlanner(select, save) {
  return (lessons, budget) => {
    const plan = select(lessons, budget);
    save(plan);
    return plan;
  };
}

Judge the design through a change

Consider adding shortest-first planning and offline storage. Trace which modules change with inheritance and which change with composition. Prefer a structure that keeps independent decisions independent while preserving a readable ordinary call path. More abstractions can increase navigation and configuration costs, so a flexible-looking diagram is not enough evidence that a design is useful.

Write a short decision record with the chosen relationship, the alternatives, and a trigger for reconsideration. Include a situation where inheritance is appropriate, such as a stable extension interface that explicitly expects subclasses. This prevents a guideline from becoming a slogan. The practical objective is predictable behavior for callers and manageable changes for maintainers, demonstrated with examples rather than an elaborate hierarchy.

Common pitfalls

  • Using inheritance because records share a few properties.
  • Creating one subclass for each combination of unrelated policies.

Retrieve what you learned

1. What matters most for a subtype?

  1. A related name
  2. Honoring the base behavior contract
  3. Having more fields
  4. Using super often
Answer and reasoning

B. Substitutability concerns observable behavior.

2. How can selection and storage vary independently?

  1. One subclass per combination
  2. Separate injected collaborators
  3. One global switch
  4. Copying the planner
Answer and reasoning

B. Composition decouples independent policies.

STAGE 3 / LESSON 16

Modules & Public Interfaces

Make dependencies and exported promises visible.

Read: Ch. 10 · Modules · §§10.1–10.3
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Define module APIs with explicit exports.
  • Explain scope and live imported bindings.
  • Control startup effects at the application boundary.

Exports define a vocabulary

A module exposes selected bindings and keeps other declarations local. Exports become the vocabulary other files use to request behavior. A planning module might export planSession and summarizeProgress while retaining its sorting helper privately. Exporting every helper turns implementation choices into accidental promises and makes later refactoring spread across unrelated consumers.

Start with one cohesive responsibility and one usage example per export. Static imports reveal dependencies near the top of a file and help tools analyze the module graph. Runtime loading rules still matter: browser and Node.js projects need compatible paths and configuration. Keep host APIs out of reusable calculations when those calculations should run in more than one environment without special setup.

Imports are live bindings

An ES module import remains connected to its exported binding. It is not a detached copy that an importer can reassign freely. If the exporter changes a mutable exported binding, importers can observe that change. This behavior does not make shared mutable exports a good default; unclear ownership still produces difficult interactions across otherwise well-separated files.

Top-level module code can have effects when the module loads. A subscription, timer, or request at import time complicates reuse and testing because a simple dependency declaration now starts work. Export an explicit start or initialize operation when startup needs control. Assign cleanup responsibility for every resource that outlives one call, and make ordinary utility imports predictable.

// planner.js
export function totalMinutes(lessons) {
  return lessons.reduce((sum, lesson) => sum + lesson.minutes, 0);
}
// app.js
import { totalMinutes } from "./planner.js";

Contracts outlive implementation details

A module interface includes argument shapes, return values, mutation rules, failures, and whether work is asynchronous. Review exports through real consumer examples. If a consumer needs an internal helper only to reconstruct a higher-level operation, the public API may be missing that operation. Alternatively, the files may not represent independent responsibilities yet and can remain together.

Draw the dependency graph and inspect cycles. Circular dependencies are supported in some forms, but initialization and availability can become subtle. Prefer a clear direction when the domain allows it, moving genuinely shared concepts into a lower-level module. A tidy diagram is useful only if the actual contracts remain clear and the boundaries correspond to coherent work that callers need. Keep one runnable consumer example beside the interface documentation so changes can be checked against an actual caller.

Common pitfalls

  • Exporting mutable state without ownership rules.
  • Starting requests or timers during an otherwise ordinary import.

Retrieve what you learned

1. ES module imports are generally what?

  1. Detached snapshots
  2. Live bindings
  3. Automatically global
  4. Writable copies
Answer and reasoning

B. Imports stay connected to exported bindings.

2. What improves testable startup?

  1. Import-time effects
  2. An explicit start function
  3. Hidden getter effects
  4. Circular imports
Answer and reasoning

B. Explicit startup gives applications and tests control.

Practice in your own editor

1. Extract modules

Split model, planning, and presentation responsibilities.

Acceptance criteria
  • Imports follow a clear direction.
  • Every export has a usage example.

2. Effects audit

Classify every top-level statement.

Acceptance criteria
  • Resource startup is explicit.
  • Cleanup has an owner.

3. API reduction

Remove unnecessary public helpers.

Acceptance criteria
  • Consumers retain useful operations.
  • Implementation details stay private.

Take it with you

  • Exports are public contracts.
  • Imports remain live.
  • Startup effects need explicit ownership.
STAGE 3 / LESSON 17

Dependency Design & Boundaries

Keep the core stable while adapters change.

Read: Ch. 10 · Modules · Module design workshop · Chapter 10
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Separate domain behavior from environment integration.
  • Inject narrow storage and clock adapters.
  • Assign recovery decisions to clear boundaries.

Dependency direction shows responsibility

A dependency means one component requires knowledge from another. A calculation that imports the DOM becomes tied to a browser even when its rule has nothing to do with a document. Move environment integration toward the application edge. Let the domain receive ordinary values and return ordinary results, while adapters translate events, storage records, and network messages.

Draw domain, adapter, and startup boxes. Place each existing operation in one box and justify the choice. Startup can connect browser persistence to a pure planner without the planner importing that implementation. Add a layer only when it clarifies a real responsibility or controls a troublesome dependency. Extra indirection without an understandable purpose makes the system harder to navigate.

Adapters translate complete contracts

A storage interface needs more than load and save names. Define missing-data behavior, malformed-data errors, synchronous or asynchronous execution, and whether saves replace or merge. An in-memory test adapter should honor the same observable contract as the real one. A fake that always returns success cannot expose the recovery behavior the application promises when persistence fails.

Use shared examples across implementations: save then load preserves the intended record, an unknown key follows the absence policy, and a failed save never claims success. Inject time where it affects decisions. A supplied clock lets examples represent expiry and deadlines without waiting or depending on the computer's current date. These explicit inputs make environmental assumptions reviewable and reproducible.

export function createSummaryService({ loadProgress, summarize }) {
  return async learnerId => {
    const progress = await loadProgress(learnerId);
    return summarize(progress);
  };
}

Contain a source of change

Consider replacing local persistence with a remote service. Transport and latency change, and previously synchronous work may become asynchronous. A domain function that already accepts data and returns a plan can remain intact while orchestration changes. If calculations read storage directly, the same transport change spreads through unrelated business logic and increases the number of behaviors you must retest.

Write an architecture note containing the graph, adapter contracts, and one complete sequence. Include failure ownership: the adapter detects malformed storage, orchestration chooses recovery, and the interface communicates the outcome. Avoid logging one error at every layer or leaving recovery to nobody. Review the note against executable examples and remove abstractions whose purpose cannot be demonstrated through a relevant change.

Common pitfalls

  • Using a fake adapter with behavior unlike production.
  • Reading environment state inside domain calculations.

Retrieve what you learned

1. Why inject a clock?

  1. To stop global time
  2. To control time-dependent examples
  3. To avoid all functions
  4. To convert dates into strings
Answer and reasoning

B. A controlled clock makes time decisions reproducible.

2. What should interchangeable adapters share?

  1. Source code
  2. Observable contracts
  3. Private field names
  4. File paths
Answer and reasoning

B. Behavioral agreement enables replacement.

Practice in your own editor

1. Dependency map

Draw the module graph and locate environment knowledge.

Acceptance criteria
  • Every arrow has a reason.
  • Core calculations run without a browser.

2. Storage contract

Implement memory persistence with explicit absence and failure behavior.

Acceptance criteria
  • Round trips preserve data.
  • Missing keys are specified.

3. Replacement trial

Substitute an asynchronous adapter.

Acceptance criteria
  • Domain rules remain focused.
  • Recovery ownership is clear.

Take it with you

  • Keep environment knowledge at boundaries.
  • Adapters must agree on behavior.
  • Useful architecture localizes change.
STAGE 3 / LESSON 18

Architecture Studio

Build a modular planner with two real consumers.

Read: Ch. 9–10 · Classes and Modules · Integration studio · Chapters 9–10
Suggested session: 100 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Deliver stable public contracts across modules.
  • Choose state ownership deliberately.
  • Demonstrate architecture through a controlled change.

Build a vertical slice

A vertical slice runs from input through domain behavior to a visible result. Give your planner two consumers: a text report and a programmatic interface. Both should call the same domain operations.
