This proves reuse with working behavior instead of a large collection of abstractions that no caller needs. Keep the first slice small enough to inspect completely.

Write acceptance scenarios for a new learner, partial progress, and a completed curriculum. Each scenario should exercise the real module wiring. Use fixtures whose expected results can be calculated manually. Add one malformed record and verify rejection at the intended boundary. A collection of isolated helper tests cannot prove that the actual application connects those helpers correctly or reports failures coherently.

Choose ownership before syntax

Use records for transferable data, functions for calculations, and a class or closure when one identity owns coordinated state. These tools can coexist. A progress store can own persistence while a pure planner calculates recommendations. Do not turn every record into a class to demonstrate syntax; require each abstraction to clarify ownership, preserve invariants, or expose meaningful behavior.

The entry point constructs adapters and connects services. Reusable modules should not secretly import startup state. If a cycle appears, inspect whether responsibilities are entangled or whether a shared concept belongs below both modules. Keep the final graph small enough to explain honestly in one diagram. Omitted dependencies make the diagram prettier but undermine its value as evidence.

// Startup owns concrete wiring.
const plan = selectLessons(curriculum, progress, budget);
const report = formatPlan(plan);
console.log(report);

Prove the design with change

Replace one policy after the first slice works. Switch from curriculum order to shortest-first planning, or replace memory storage with another contract-compatible adapter. Record which modules changed and why. A useful boundary contains the relevant change while unrelated domain behavior remains correct. If edits spread everywhere, repair the dependency direction before adding more features on top of it.

Score correctness at forty percent, boundary clarity at twenty-five, the change demonstration at twenty, and documentation at fifteen. Deliver a run guide, exported API examples, a dependency diagram, and a decision record. Include one limitation and a condition for revisiting the design. The evidence should show that the application solves its current problem and that its abstractions earn their cost.

Common pitfalls

  • Treating unused abstractions as proof of flexibility.
  • Testing helpers without exercising actual module wiring.

Retrieve what you learned

1. What demonstrates a useful boundary?

  1. More directories
  2. A relevant change stays localized
  3. Every record is a class
  4. No imports
Answer and reasoning

B. A boundary is valuable when it contains a meaningful source of change.

2. Where should concrete wiring usually happen?

  1. Inside every calculation
  2. Application startup
  3. A hidden getter
  4. An arbitrary global
Answer and reasoning

B. The entry point can assemble dependencies explicitly.

Practice in your own editor

1. Two consumers

Run the planner through text and programmatic interfaces.

Acceptance criteria
  • Both share domain operations.
  • Acceptance fixtures pass end to end.

2. Policy replacement

Swap one strategy or adapter.

Acceptance criteria
  • Changed modules are explained.
  • Unrelated behavior remains correct.

3. Architecture dossier

Deliver a run guide, graph, contracts, and decision record.

Acceptance criteria
  • The weighted rubric is scored.
  • A limitation and revisit trigger are stated.

Take it with you

  • Working consumers prove reuse.
  • Ownership guides abstraction choices.
  • Demonstrate change instead of promising it.
STAGE 4 / LESSON 19

The Standard Library Toolkit

Choose collections and binary representations by their behavior.

Read: Ch. 11 · The JavaScript Standard Library · §§11.1–11.2, 11.6, 11.9
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Choose Map and Set for appropriate collection semantics.
  • Distinguish structured data from serialized text.
  • Recognize when typed arrays and URL objects are useful.

Choose a collection by the question

A Set stores unique values and supports membership checks without manually searching an array. A Map associates keys with values and allows keys beyond strings and symbols. Plain objects remain useful for records with known fields. Select the structure by the operations and meaning you need: a lesson record, a set of completed identifiers, and a map from identifier to lesson serve different purposes.

Object keys in a Map use identity, so two equivalent-looking records are still different keys. Set membership has similar identity implications for objects. Prefer stable primitive identifiers when data crosses serialization boundaries. A recreated object will not match the identity of an earlier object merely because their fields agree. Write examples that distinguish duplicate primitives from separately created object values.

Serialization changes representation

JSON converts a supported data structure into text and parses text into new values. It does not preserve every JavaScript feature. Functions, undefined values, special numeric values, dates, maps, sets, and cycles require particular care or explicit conversion policies. Parsing successfully only establishes valid JSON syntax; it does not prove that the result matches your application schema or is safe to use.

Treat serialization as a boundary. Define a plain transfer shape, serialize it, parse it, and validate it before creating domain values. Include a version when the shape may evolve. Test round trips using the actual supported values, and do not use JSON serialization as a universal deep-cloning trick. Representation changes can silently remove information that your program depends on.

const completed = new Set(["L1", "L1", "L2"]);
const byId = new Map(lessons.map(lesson => [lesson.id, lesson]));
const url = new URL("https://example.com/learn");
url.searchParams.set("stage", "2");

Use specialized tools deliberately

Typed arrays provide views of numeric elements over binary memory buffers. They are useful for binary formats, media, and APIs that exchange bytes, while ordinary arrays are more flexible for general application records. URL and URLSearchParams provide structured handling of addresses and query parameters, avoiding fragile string concatenation and manual escaping. Specialized tools reduce errors when their contracts match the problem.

Explore one tool at a time with a small concrete example: deduplicate completion IDs, index lessons by ID, serialize a progress record, and build a shareable filter URL. Explain the input and output representation at each step. Avoid selecting a sophisticated collection merely for novelty; the best choice makes the expected operations and identity rules obvious to the next reader.

Common pitfalls

  • Using object identity when stable IDs are needed across loads.
  • Assuming valid JSON is valid application data.

Retrieve what you learned

1. Which structure naturally represents unique completed IDs?

  1. Set
  2. Date
  3. RegExp
  4. DataView
Answer and reasoning

A. A Set directly expresses uniqueness and membership.

2. What does successful JSON.parse guarantee?

  1. Correct application schema
  2. Valid JSON syntax was parsed
  3. No missing fields
  4. Preserved prototypes
Answer and reasoning

B. The parsed value still needs domain validation.

Practice in your own editor

1. Collection choice

Implement completion membership and lesson lookup with appropriate structures.

Acceptance criteria
  • Duplicates behave intentionally.
  • Object identity implications are explained.

2. Progress transfer

Define and validate a versioned JSON progress format.

Acceptance criteria
  • A round trip preserves supported data.
  • Malformed records are rejected.

3. Shareable filters

Build and parse a filter URL with URLSearchParams.

Acceptance criteria
  • Special characters round-trip.
  • Missing parameters have explicit defaults.

Take it with you

  • Choose structures by semantics.
  • Serialization requires a transfer contract.
  • Specialized APIs can replace fragile manual parsing.
STAGE 4 / LESSON 20

Text, Dates & Internationalization

Handle patterns, time, and presentation without hidden assumptions.

Read: Ch. 11 · The JavaScript Standard Library · §§11.3–11.4, 11.7
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Use regular expressions for bounded text patterns.
  • Separate timestamps from localized presentation.
  • Format numbers and dates using explicit locale decisions.

Patterns are small parsers with limits

A regular expression describes a pattern in text. Anchors constrain where a match occurs, character classes describe allowed characters, and quantifiers specify repetition. Use a regex when the pattern is small and understandable. Complex nested data or a rich grammar usually deserves a parser. A concise pattern is not automatically readable, correct, or safe for every input size.

Write accepted and rejected examples before the pattern, including empty input and boundary lengths. Decide whether the entire string must match or whether a substring is enough. Flags change behavior, and global or sticky expressions maintain lastIndex state across relevant operations. Avoid reusing a stateful regex casually as if every test were independent. Explain each part of the pattern in ordinary language.

A timestamp is not a calendar policy

A Date represents an instant as a numeric time value, while its formatting and component access can depend on a time zone. Calendar dates, local appointment times, and elapsed durations are different concepts. Adding a fixed number of milliseconds is suitable for an elapsed duration but may not implement a local calendar-day rule around daylight-saving transitions or other offset changes.

Store and exchange timestamps in an explicit format, and decide which time zone the product uses for calendar interpretation. Avoid ambiguous date strings whose parsing assumptions are unclear. Inject the current time into rules so boundary tests are deterministic. Include examples near midnight and a relevant offset transition when a feature promises calendar behavior rather than simply measuring elapsed milliseconds.

const formatter = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-GB", {
  dateStyle: "medium", timeZone: "UTC"
});
console.log(formatter.format(new Date("2026-01-15T12:00:00Z")));

Presentation belongs at a boundary

Intl formatters express locale-sensitive number and date presentation without manually assembling punctuation or month names. Keep domain values numeric or structured until the presentation boundary. A formatted currency string is a display value, not a reliable input for arithmetic. Likewise, do not compare localized date strings to decide which event occurred first; compare appropriate time values instead.

Create reusable formatters for a chosen locale and explicit time zone when consistency matters. Compare two locales to observe differences in grouping, decimal separators, and date order. Your tests should distinguish semantic correctness from exact presentation expectations. Record whether a product follows the viewer's preferences or an organization-wide setting so the same timestamp does not appear mysteriously inconsistent across screens.

Common pitfalls

  • Treating localized display strings as arithmetic or sorting values.
  • Assuming an elapsed twenty-four hours always means the next local calendar day.

Retrieve what you learned

1. What should be compared to order instants?

  1. Localized display strings
  2. Their numeric time values
  3. Month names
  4. String lengths
Answer and reasoning

B. Numeric timestamps represent chronological order without locale formatting ambiguity.

2. Why can a reused global regex surprise you?

  1. It changes the source text
  2. It maintains lastIndex state
  3. It becomes asynchronous
  4. It ignores all anchors
Answer and reasoning

B. Global and sticky expressions can retain position state between operations.

Practice in your own editor

1. Identifier pattern

Validate a deliberately limited lesson-code format.

Acceptance criteria
  • Accepted and rejected examples precede the regex.
  • The full-string policy is explicit.

2. Deadline boundary

Implement a deadline rule with an injected current time.

Acceptance criteria
  • Before, exactly at, and after the deadline are covered.
  • Time representation is documented.

3. Locale gallery

Render one amount and one timestamp in three locales.

Acceptance criteria
  • Domain values remain unchanged.
  • Time-zone policy is explicit.

Take it with you

  • Regex patterns need examples and limits.
  • Instants, durations, and calendar rules differ.
  • Format at the presentation boundary.
STAGE 4 / LESSON 21

Iterators & Generators

Process sequences lazily through a shared protocol.

Read: Ch. 12 · Iterators and Generators · §§12.1–12.4
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Distinguish an iterable from an iterator.
  • Use generators to express lazy sequences.
  • Explain exhaustion and cleanup during iteration.

Iteration is a protocol

An iterable supplies a method at Symbol.iterator that returns an iterator. An iterator supplies next, whose result describes a value and whether iteration is done. for...of and spread consume this protocol. A collection can create a fresh iterator for each traversal, while an iterator commonly represents one evolving position. These are related roles, not interchangeable guarantees of repeatable iteration.

Inspect a built-in iterator manually by calling next several times. Record the value and done fields, including the exhausted state. Then compare consuming the same iterator twice with requesting a new iterator from the original collection. This experiment explains why a function accepting an arbitrary iterable should not assume it can traverse the input repeatedly without documenting that requirement.

Generators describe suspended computation

A generator function returns a generator object when called. Its body advances when the consumer requests the next item, suspending at yield. Local variables remain available between resumptions, which makes stateful sequence logic readable. A range generator can produce values without first allocating an array for the entire range. Laziness changes when work happens and can reduce memory requirements.

Laziness does not automatically make every algorithm faster. Repeated consumption may repeat computation, and a consumer that spreads an infinite generator into an array never finishes. Define whether a sequence is finite and how a consumer can stop. Use generators when the incremental nature of the data improves the model, such as traversing pages or producing records as they become available.

function* range(start, end) {
  for (let value = start; value < end; value++) yield value;
}
const iterator = range(2, 4);
console.log(iterator.next()); // { value: 2, done: false }

Composition needs termination and cleanup

Generator helpers can map, filter, or limit a sequence while preserving lazy evaluation. A take helper should consume only the requested number of items and handle zero cleanly. Early termination matters when the source owns resources. Iteration protocols can support cleanup through return, and a generator can use try/finally to release resources when consumption closes it appropriately.

Build an instrumented source that logs each produced value, then apply a filter and a limit. Compare the produced count with the returned count; filtering may require examining more items than the output contains. Document this distinction when work is expensive. Test empty input, exhaustion, early stopping, and a consumer exception so your abstraction does not accidentally promise a simpler lifecycle than it implements.

Common pitfalls

  • Assuming every iterator can be restarted.
  • Materializing an unbounded sequence with spread.

Retrieve what you learned

1. What does calling a generator function immediately return?

  1. Its final value
  2. A generator object
  3. An array of all yields
  4. A Promise in every case
Answer and reasoning

B. The generator object advances its body as iteration requests values.

2. Why distinguish iterable from iterator?

  1. They are unrelated
  2. An iterable can provide fresh traversal while an iterator tracks progress
  3. Only arrays are iterable
  4. Iterators cannot end
Answer and reasoning

B. A sequence source and one traversal state have different lifecycle properties.

Practice in your own editor

1. Manual protocol

Consume an array iterator using next and record every result.

Acceptance criteria
  • Exhaustion is observed.
  • Fresh and reused iterators are compared.

2. Lazy toolkit

Implement generator-based map and take helpers.

Acceptance criteria
  • Zero and empty cases work.
  • The source is not fully materialized.

3. Production audit

Instrument a filtered sequence and measure produced versus returned values.

Acceptance criteria
  • Early stopping is visible.
  • Cleanup behavior is documented.

Take it with you

  • Iteration is a shared protocol.
  • Generators suspend computation between requests.
  • Laziness needs explicit termination assumptions.
STAGE 4 / LESSON 22

Promises & Failure Semantics

Reason about eventual values and connected error paths.

Read: Ch. 13 · Asynchronous JavaScript · §§13.1–13.2
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Trace fulfillment, rejection, and chained promises.
  • Return asynchronous work so callers can observe it.
  • Distinguish recovery from accidental error swallowing.

A promise represents an eventual outcome

A promise begins pending and eventually fulfills with a value or rejects with a reason. Its state settles once. Attaching handlers observes that outcome without blocking the current stack. A promise is not the result itself, and creating one does not automatically move CPU work onto another thread. The surrounding API determines what work occurs and how it is scheduled.

Draw a timeline with synchronous statements and promise reactions. Handlers run after the current synchronous work completes according to the host's scheduling model. Predict a simple log order before running it. Keep the distinction between starting an operation and observing its promise: a request may already be in flight before you attach a handler or pass the promise to another function.

Chains connect values and failures

then returns a new promise. Returning a plain value fulfills that next promise with the value; returning a promise adopts its eventual outcome. Throwing inside a handler rejects the next promise. This is why return is essential when a handler begins another asynchronous operation. Without it, the outer chain may finish before the nested work and cannot reliably observe its result or failure.

Keep each step focused on one transformation. Name the intermediate result and specify whether it is immediate or eventual. A catch handler that returns a value converts rejection into fulfillment, which is a recovery policy. If recovery is impossible, rethrow or let the rejection propagate. Logging an error and returning nothing can accidentally make a failed operation appear successfully completed with undefined.

loadProgress()
  .then(progress => savePlan(buildPlan(progress)))
  .then(() => console.log("Saved"))
  .catch(error => console.error("Plan failed:", error.message));

Completion and cleanup are different concerns

finally is useful for cleanup that should happen after fulfillment or rejection. It does not receive the successful value or rejection reason as its argument. A failure thrown during cleanup can replace the earlier outcome, so cleanup deserves its own contract. Avoid using finally to manufacture success or to hide an error that the caller still needs to handle.

At the application boundary, attach a deliberate rejection path. Record what the user sees, which diagnostics remain available, and whether retry is appropriate. Test a failure at each asynchronous step rather than only rejecting the first request. The chain should connect all work that belongs to the operation, and its returned promise should settle only when the operation's promised responsibility is complete.

Common pitfalls

  • Starting nested async work without returning its promise.
  • Catching a failure and unintentionally converting it into success.

Retrieve what you learned

1. What happens when a then handler throws?

  1. The process always stops immediately
  2. The next promise rejects
  3. The error disappears
  4. The original value is returned
Answer and reasoning

B. Thrown handler errors become rejections in the chained promise.

2. What does returning a fallback from catch do?

  1. Keeps the chain rejected
  2. Recovers into fulfillment with that value
  3. Cancels all work
  4. Retries automatically
Answer and reasoning

B. A normal return from catch produces a fulfilled continuation.

Practice in your own editor

1. Timeline prediction

Predict and verify a mixed synchronous and promise log sequence.

Acceptance criteria
  • The current stack is distinguished from reactions.
  • Each output position is explained.

2. Broken chain repair

Repair nested asynchronous work whose promise is not returned.

Acceptance criteria
  • The caller waits for all promised work.
  • Nested failure reaches the boundary.

3. Recovery policy

Implement one recoverable failure and one propagated failure.

Acceptance criteria
  • Fallback behavior is explicit.
  • Logging does not silently manufacture success.

Take it with you

  • Promises represent eventual outcomes.
  • Return work to connect the chain.
  • catch can recover; recovery must be intentional.
STAGE 4 / LESSON 23

Async Workflows & Concurrency

Control overlap, failure, and cancellation deliberately.

Read: Ch. 13 · Asynchronous JavaScript · §§13.2.5, 13.3; concurrency workshop
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Use async/await without losing error semantics.
  • Choose sequential or concurrent execution intentionally.
  • Bound concurrency and handle stale results.

Await makes suspension readable

An async function always returns a promise. await pauses that function's continuation until its operand settles, while other work can proceed in the environment. A rejection at await behaves like a thrown error inside the async function and can be handled with try/catch. This syntax makes asynchronous control flow resemble ordinary sequencing, but it does not turn an eventual result into a synchronous return value.

Trace both the caller and callee. Calling an async function gives the caller a promise immediately; awaiting it connects the caller's continuation to the outcome. Avoid mixing awaited and unobserved work accidentally. If a background operation is intentional, give it its own failure handling and lifecycle. Otherwise return or await it so the function's promise accurately represents the responsibility its name suggests.

Overlap independent work deliberately

Sequential awaits are appropriate when a later step depends on an earlier result. Independent operations can be started together and observed with Promise.all. Promise.all rejects when one input rejects, but it does not cancel the remaining work. Promise.allSettled collects every outcome when partial results are useful. Choose the combinator from the product's failure policy rather than treating concurrency as an automatic speed improvement.

Unbounded concurrency can overload a service or consume too much memory. A worker pool limits the number of active operations while preserving a defined output order. Separate concurrency, rate limits, and total work: limiting active requests does not necessarily limit requests per second. Start with a small pool and instrument active counts so the bound is supported by evidence instead of assumed from the code.

const [lessons, progress] = await Promise.all([
  loadLessons(),
  loadProgress()
]);
const plan = buildPlan(lessons, progress);

Cancellation and stale results need ownership

Cancellation is cooperative: an operation must support and observe a cancellation signal. Aborting a request does not retroactively undo every side effect or settle unrelated work. A browser search interface also needs stale-result protection, because an earlier request can finish after a newer one. Use a request identity or equivalent state check before committing a response to current UI state.

Test timing with controlled deferred promises rather than relying on random delays. Resolve requests in reverse order, reject one worker, and cancel an operation while another is active. Specify whether partial results are retained and what cleanup occurs. These examples expose race conditions that a normal fast connection often hides, and they turn concurrency from a vague performance feature into an explicit behavioral contract.

Common pitfalls

  • Assuming Promise.all cancels remaining operations after rejection.
  • Letting an older request overwrite newer interface state.

Retrieve what you learned

1. When one Promise.all input rejects, what is guaranteed?

  1. All work is canceled
  2. The aggregate rejects
  3. All inputs stop running
  4. Partial values are returned
Answer and reasoning

B. The aggregate rejects, but ongoing operations are not automatically canceled.

2. Why use a request identity in live search?

  1. To sort alphabetically
  2. To prevent stale responses from replacing newer results
  3. To encrypt queries
  4. To make fetch synchronous
Answer and reasoning

B. An identity check connects a response to the currently relevant request.

Practice in your own editor

1. Sequential versus parallel

Implement dependent and independent loading examples.

Acceptance criteria
  • Dependencies determine sequencing.
  • Failure behavior is documented.

2. Worker pool

Process a collection with a concurrency limit of three.

Acceptance criteria
  • Active work never exceeds three.
  • Output order is defined.

3. Race laboratory

Resolve two searches in reverse order.

Acceptance criteria
  • Only the latest request can commit results.
  • Cancellation and failure paths are covered.

Take it with you

  • async functions return promises.
  • Concurrency needs bounds and failure policy.
  • Stale-result protection is separate from cancellation.
STAGE 4 / LESSON 24

Resilient Data Pipeline Studio

Combine validation, lazy processing, and controlled async work.

Read: Ch. 11–13 · Standard Library, Iteration, and Async · Integration studio · Chapters 11–13
Suggested session: 110 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Build a staged pipeline with explicit representations.
  • Bound concurrent work and report partial failures.
  • Deliver operational evidence for cancellation and retries.

Define the pipeline as contracts

Build an importer for lesson-resource metadata. The source supplies records, validation checks their shape, normalization creates domain values, enrichment fetches additional information, and reporting summarizes results. Write the input and output shape of each stage. Distinguish a malformed record from a network failure and from an empty but valid source. These situations need different reporting and recovery decisions.

Use stable identifiers to deduplicate records with Set or Map according to your duplicate policy. Decide whether the first record wins, the last record wins, or duplicates are rejected. Preserve source context such as an index or identifier so a failure can be traced to its origin. Avoid reducing every error to a single count that leaves the user unable to repair the input.

Control resources and partial outcomes

Process records incrementally when the source is large, and bound enrichment concurrency. Define whether the pipeline stops on the first failure or continues collecting per-record outcomes. A report can contain successes, rejected records, and failed enrichments without pretending that partial completion is total success. Keep cancellation ownership at the operation boundary and pass signals only to work that supports them.

Retries require a reason and a limit. Retry transient operations only when repeating them is safe, and do not retry malformed input as if time would fix it. Separate attempts from unique records in metrics. A useful report shows how many records were read, accepted, enriched, and failed, plus the maximum observed concurrency. These measurements reveal whether the implementation honors its operational promises.

An asynchronous iterable extends the sequence model to values that arrive over time. for await...of waits for successive items while preserving readable loop control. It suits a streamed source, but does not automatically make downstream processing concurrent. Keep source iteration, worker scheduling, and cancellation as separate responsibilities so the pipeline can explain both ordering and resource use.

const report = { read: 0, accepted: 0, succeeded: 0, failed: [] };
// Each accepted record must reach exactly one terminal outcome.
// Record source identifiers alongside failures for repair.

Demonstrate resilience with controlled failures

Create fixtures for an empty source, duplicates, malformed records, one transient failure, one permanent failure, and cancellation midway through processing. Use deterministic test doubles to control resolution order. Verify that every accepted record reaches exactly one terminal outcome and that no new work starts after your cancellation policy takes effect. Explain any already-running work that is allowed to finish.

Score correctness at thirty-five percent, failure handling at thirty, resource control at twenty, and reporting at fifteen. Deliver the importer, fixtures, a sample report, and a short operations note. The note should explain retry limits, cancellation behavior, and how to interpret partial results. A polished success demo is useful, but the distinguishing evidence is a clear account of what happens when the source or network misbehaves.

Common pitfalls

  • Retrying invalid records indefinitely.
  • Reporting partial completion as unconditional success.

Retrieve what you learned

1. What makes a retry policy defensible?

  1. Retry everything forever
  2. Transient failure, safe repetition, and a bound
  3. Only a delay
  4. Ignoring failed attempts
Answer and reasoning

B. Retries need a reason, safe semantics, and a stopping rule.

2. What should each accepted record reach?

  1. An arbitrary number of successes
  2. Exactly one terminal outcome
  3. Only a console message
  4. No result if it fails
Answer and reasoning

B. Terminal accounting makes partial outcomes auditable.

Practice in your own editor

1. Pipeline contracts

Specify validation, normalization, deduplication, and enrichment stages.

Acceptance criteria
  • Each representation is documented.
  • Duplicate behavior is explicit.

2. Failure fixtures

Implement deterministic transient, permanent, and canceled scenarios.

Acceptance criteria
  • Retries stop at a bound.
  • Every accepted record is accounted for.

3. Operations report

Deliver metrics and a sample partial-failure report.

Acceptance criteria
  • Maximum concurrency is measured.
  • Failures include repairable source context.
  • The weighted rubric is scored.

Take it with you

  • Each pipeline stage owns a clear contract.
  • Resource limits need measurements.
  • Resilience is demonstrated through controlled failures.
STAGE 5 / LESSON 25

The Browser Execution Model

Understand how scripts, tasks, rendering, and documents interact.

Read: Ch. 15 · JavaScript in Web Browsers · §§15.1–15.2
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Separate the language runtime from browser capabilities.
  • Explain task and microtask ordering in small examples.
  • Load scripts without assuming unavailable DOM state.

The browser hosts several cooperating systems

A browser combines JavaScript execution with document parsing, styling, layout, rendering, networking, and user interaction. Your script sees host APIs that coordinate these systems, but a long synchronous calculation can still prevent the main thread from responding promptly. An asynchronous network API avoids waiting synchronously for the network; it does not make every callback or subsequent calculation inexpensive.

Draw a timeline for a page that loads data and renders a list. Mark parsing, script execution, request completion, state updates, and rendering opportunities. This diagram helps explain why changing the DOM does not necessarily mean the user sees pixels immediately. Performance work begins by identifying which system is busy and which thread owns the work, not by adding arbitrary timers.

Tasks and microtasks affect observation

Browser events and timers schedule tasks, while promise reactions use the microtask mechanism. After the current stack completes, microtasks are processed at appropriate checkpoints before the browser continues its event-loop work. A chain of microtasks can delay other work, so repeatedly scheduling promises is not a reliable way to yield for rendering. Timers also express a minimum delay, not an exact appointment.

Predict the output of a synchronous log, a resolved-promise handler, and a zero-delay timer. Then run the example and explain the order. Keep the model modest: do not infer precise frame timing from one console trace. Use the model to distinguish guaranteed ordering within your code from host scheduling details that require measurement or a more specific API contract.

console.log("sync");
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("microtask"));
setTimeout(() => console.log("timer task"), 0);

Startup must match document availability

A script can run before the elements it needs have been parsed. Script placement and loading attributes influence when execution occurs, and module scripts have their own loading behavior. Choose an explicit startup strategy rather than treating a null query result as a mysterious intermittent bug. Keep initialization idempotent where repeated setup is possible, and avoid registering the same listeners more than once.

Build a startup checklist: required root element exists, configuration is parsed, initial state is established, listeners are attached, and the first render occurs. Define cleanup if the application can be mounted and unmounted. Test an empty document root and a failed initial request. The loading and failure states belong to the interface contract just as much as the final successful screen.

Common pitfalls

  • Assuming a zero-delay timer runs immediately or at an exact time.
  • Querying elements before the chosen startup strategy makes them available.

Retrieve what you learned

1. Which work can block main-thread interaction?

  1. A long synchronous callback
  2. A pending request alone
  3. A CSS class name
  4. An uncalled function
Answer and reasoning

A. Long synchronous JavaScript occupies the main thread.

2. What does a zero-delay timer guarantee?

  1. Immediate execution
  2. Scheduling after a minimum delay subject to the event loop
  3. Exact rendering order
  4. A new worker thread
Answer and reasoning

B. A timer is scheduled; it does not interrupt the current stack or promise exact timing.

Practice in your own editor

1. Event-loop notebook

Predict five small task and microtask sequences.

Acceptance criteria
  • Predictions precede execution.
  • Guarantees are separated from timing observations.

2. Startup experiment

Compare script loading before and after required elements exist.

Acceptance criteria
  • The null-query cause is explained.
  • The final startup strategy is explicit.

3. Loading states

Render initial, loading, success, and failure states.

Acceptance criteria
  • The UI never depends on invisible initialization assumptions.
  • Retry does not duplicate listeners.

Take it with you

  • Browser systems share constrained resources.
  • Task ordering differs from exact timing.
  • Startup and failure states are part of the product.
STAGE 5 / LESSON 26

DOM as a Render Target

Translate application state into safe, predictable interface updates.

Read: Ch. 15 · JavaScript in Web Browsers · §§15.3–15.4
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Query and create DOM nodes with deliberate ownership.
  • Render text without interpreting untrusted markup.
  • Keep state and the displayed document consistent.

The document is a tree of nodes

DOM APIs expose a mutable tree representing the document. Query methods find nodes, creation methods construct nodes, and insertion methods connect them. A selector can return no match, one element, or a collection depending on the API. Know whether a returned collection is live or static before assuming it will reflect later changes. The tree is an interface representation, not automatically your application model.

Choose one root that your component owns. Keep queries scoped to that root where possible, and avoid modifying unrelated page areas. Create a small lesson-card renderer that receives a record and returns a node. This boundary makes the renderer easy to exercise with fixtures and lets callers decide where the node belongs. Clear ownership reduces accidental cross-component updates.

Text and markup require different trust

textContent inserts text without treating it as HTML. innerHTML parses markup, which creates a different trust boundary when content comes from users, remote services, or imported files. For ordinary lesson titles and descriptions, use text nodes or textContent. Building interface elements through DOM methods also makes attribute and event behavior explicit rather than embedding uncontrolled strings in a large template.

If a feature truly accepts rich markup, it needs a deliberate sanitization and rendering policy rather than improvised string replacement. Keep this lesson focused on plain text rendering and safe attribute choices. Test a title containing angle brackets, quotation marks, and an apparent script tag. The expected behavior is to display the characters as text, not execute or reinterpret them as page structure.

function lessonCard(lesson) {
  const article = document.createElement("article");
  const title = document.createElement("h2");
  title.textContent = lesson.title;
  article.append(title);
  return article;
}

Render from state with intentional updates

A simple renderer can derive the entire owned subtree from application state. Replacing everything is easy to reason about, but can disrupt focus, selection, scroll position, and in-progress input. More selective updates preserve interaction state but require careful reconciliation. Choose the smallest approach that preserves the behavior your interface promises, and test those behaviors rather than measuring quality only by the number of DOM operations.

Avoid alternating layout reads and writes unnecessarily in large loops. Batch related changes and inspect performance before optimizing. Track list items by stable identifiers when their order changes, and preserve focused controls during updates. A correct renderer should handle an empty list, repeated updates, long text, and changed ordering while keeping the visible document consistent with the underlying model.

Common pitfalls

  • Rendering user-controlled strings with innerHTML.
  • Replacing focused form controls during every unrelated state update.

Retrieve what you learned

1. Which API displays a title as plain text?

  1. innerHTML
  2. textContent
  3. eval
  4. document.write
Answer and reasoning

B. textContent does not parse the value as HTML markup.

2. What can whole-subtree replacement disrupt?

  1. Only colors
  2. Focus and in-progress input
  3. JavaScript syntax
  4. The language type system
Answer and reasoning

B. Replacing nodes can discard interaction state even when the new screen looks similar.

Practice in your own editor

1. Safe cards

Render lesson cards containing punctuation and markup-like text.

Acceptance criteria
  • Text is displayed literally.
  • Queries stay within an owned root.

2. State renderer

Render empty, populated, and reordered lesson collections.

Acceptance criteria
  • Stable IDs identify records.
  • Repeated renders remain consistent.

3. Focus preservation

Update a summary while a user edits an input.

Acceptance criteria
  • The input retains focus and its draft value.
  • The update strategy is explained.

Take it with you

  • Own a clear DOM boundary.
  • Plain text should remain plain text.
  • Rendering correctness includes interaction state.
STAGE 5 / LESSON 27

Events, Forms & Accessibility

Design interactions that work with keyboards and real user behavior.

Read: Ch. 15 · JavaScript in Web Browsers · §§15.2–15.3; forms workshop
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Explain event propagation and delegation.
  • Use semantic form controls and clear validation.
  • Preserve keyboard and focus behavior through state changes.

Events travel through a document path

An event has a target and travels through propagation phases. A listener's currentTarget identifies the node whose listener is running, which may differ from the original target. Event delegation places a listener on a stable ancestor and determines which child action occurred. This can simplify dynamic lists, but the handler must verify that a matched action belongs to the intended component boundary.

preventDefault requests cancellation of a default action when the event supports it; stopPropagation affects propagation. These are different responsibilities. Do not call either automatically in every handler. For a form, listen to submit so keyboard submission and button activation follow the same path. Handle the event according to the product behavior rather than only the exact mouse gesture used during development.

Semantic controls carry useful behavior

Native buttons, inputs, labels, and forms provide keyboard and accessibility behavior that a clickable generic element does not automatically have. A label should identify its control, and a validation message should explain how to correct the input. Keep raw input, converted values, and validated domain values separate. A successful browser validity check does not replace the domain rules or server-side validation needed elsewhere.

Make errors local and specific: name the field, explain the problem, and retain the user's entry. For asynchronous submission, communicate pending state and prevent accidental duplicate operations without trapping the user. Decide where focus moves after success or failure. These details are part of functional correctness because they determine whether someone can complete the task without a pointer or without seeing every visual cue.

form.addEventListener("submit", event => {
  event.preventDefault();
  const raw = new FormData(form).get("minutes");
  submitValidatedMinutes(raw);
});

Test an interaction as a sequence

A button click is only one step in a larger flow. Test tabbing into the form, entering invalid data, correcting it, submitting, waiting, and returning to useful content. Dynamic feedback should be available through appropriate accessible semantics, and focus should remain visible. Avoid moving focus on every state update; move it only when the workflow requires a clear transition.

Create an interaction matrix covering keyboard, pointer, empty input, repeated submission, slow response, and failure. Use the browser's accessibility tools to inspect labels and roles, then manually complete the flow with the keyboard. Automated checks can reveal some issues, but they do not prove that the entire experience is understandable or that the chosen focus movement matches the user's task.

Common pitfalls

  • Handling only a button click and missing keyboard form submission.
  • Using clickable generic elements without equivalent keyboard semantics.

Retrieve what you learned

1. Which event naturally covers form submission by keyboard and button?

  1. mouseover
  2. submit
  3. mousemove
  4. scroll
Answer and reasoning

B. The submit event represents the form action across activation methods.

2. What does currentTarget identify?

  1. Always the deepest clicked node
  2. The node whose listener is executing
  3. The browser window always
  4. The first matching selector
Answer and reasoning

B. currentTarget refers to the listener attachment point during that handler.

Practice in your own editor

1. Delegated actions

Implement completion buttons in a dynamically updated lesson list.

Acceptance criteria
  • Nested click targets are handled.
  • Actions remain inside the component boundary.

2. Accessible planner form

Build labeled duration and goal controls with useful validation.

Acceptance criteria
  • Keyboard submission works.
  • Errors retain input and explain corrections.

3. Interaction audit

Complete the full flow using only a keyboard.

Acceptance criteria
  • Focus stays visible.
  • Pending and failed states are understandable.

Take it with you

  • Propagation and default actions are separate concepts.
  • Semantic controls provide behavior worth keeping.
  • Test complete interaction sequences.
STAGE 5 / LESSON 28

Fetch, Storage & State

Connect remote data and persistence without losing control of the UI.

Read: Ch. 15 · JavaScript in Web Browsers · §§15.11–15.12
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Handle HTTP failures separately from network failures.
  • Validate persisted data before using it.
  • Represent loading, success, and failure as explicit state.

Fetch exposes transport and response separately

fetch returns a promise for a response when the request reaches a response outcome. HTTP error statuses such as 404 do not automatically reject that promise. Check response.ok or the expected status before interpreting the body. Parsing JSON is another asynchronous step that can fail. Distinguish network failure, unsuccessful HTTP response, invalid representation, and domain-invalid data in your boundary logic.

Treat request construction as an API contract: method, URL, headers, body, and cancellation behavior should be intentional. Keep credentials and secrets out of client code. For a learning application, a read-only resource endpoint is enough to practice the lifecycle. Use controlled fixtures for success, empty data, malformed JSON, and an unsuccessful status so the interface does not only work on a perfect response.

Persistence is fallible external state

Browser storage can preserve progress between sessions, but stored values are not automatically trustworthy or compatible forever. localStorage stores strings and its operations are synchronous. Parsing or writing can fail, and users can clear storage. Define a versioned record, validate it after parsing, and choose a recovery policy for missing or malformed data. Do not let storage corruption prevent the entire interface from starting.

Keep the in-memory model authoritative during an interaction, then persist through a narrow adapter. Report a failed save honestly instead of displaying a success message merely because the checkbox changed. Decide whether the interface keeps an unsaved local change or rolls it back. Both approaches require visible state so the user can understand whether progress will survive a reload.

const response = await fetch("/api/lessons");
if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
const payload = await response.json();
const lessons = validateLessons(payload);

State should describe the whole request lifecycle

Represent request state explicitly: idle, loading, success, empty, and error may have different displays and permitted actions. A boolean loading flag plus unrelated error and data variables can create contradictory combinations unless updates are coordinated. A small discriminated state shape makes the allowed combinations easier to reason about and easier to render consistently.

Protect against stale responses when a filter or selected learner changes during a request. A response should update only the state that still owns it. Test reload recovery, failed persistence, and request completion in reverse order. The acceptance criterion is not merely that data eventually appears; the interface must remain truthful about which request the data belongs to and whether edits have been saved.

Common pitfalls

  • Assuming fetch rejects automatically on every HTTP error status.
  • Trusting stored JSON without schema and version checks.

Retrieve what you learned

1. What happens for an ordinary HTTP 404 response to fetch?

  1. It necessarily rejects
  2. It resolves to a response with unsuccessful status
  3. It returns null
  4. It retries forever
Answer and reasoning

B. HTTP status must be checked separately from network rejection.

2. What should happen after loading persisted JSON?

  1. Use it immediately
  2. Validate its version and shape
  3. Evaluate it as code
  4. Assume every field exists
Answer and reasoning

B. Persistent data can be malformed, obsolete, or missing required fields.

Practice in your own editor

1. Response matrix

Handle successful, empty, unsuccessful-status, and malformed responses.

Acceptance criteria
  • Each outcome has an explicit UI state.
  • JSON parsing failures are handled.

2. Progress adapter

Persist versioned progress with validation and recovery.

Acceptance criteria
  • Missing data initializes safely.
  • Failed saves are visible.

3. Race and reload test

Switch filters during loading and reload after saving.

Acceptance criteria
  • Stale responses cannot overwrite current state.
  • Reloaded progress matches the documented persistence policy.

Take it with you

  • HTTP failures require response checks.
  • Persistence is a boundary with failures.
  • State must tell the truth about requests and saves.
STAGE 5 / LESSON 29

Browser APIs & Responsive Work

Use capabilities progressively and keep expensive work controlled.

Read: Ch. 15 · JavaScript in Web Browsers · §§15.5–15.10, 15.13
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Select browser capabilities with feature detection.
  • Move suitable CPU work to a worker.
  • Assign cleanup and cancellation to owned resources.

Capabilities need progressive behavior

Browser APIs provide graphics, media, history, location, observers, and many other capabilities. Availability and permissions vary by environment. Feature detection asks whether a capability exists before using it; it is more reliable than assuming behavior from a browser name. A core workflow should remain understandable when an optional enhancement is unavailable, denied, or interrupted.

Choose one useful enhancement for the planner, such as a canvas progress chart or history-based navigation. Define the baseline experience first. Then specify how the enhancement improves it and what happens if it fails. Keep essential information available as text or semantic controls rather than only pixels. A capability is valuable when it supports a user task, not merely when it creates an impressive demonstration.

Workers separate suitable CPU work

A web worker executes JavaScript in a separate worker context and communicates through messages. It cannot directly manipulate the page DOM. This makes it suitable for expensive calculations that can operate on transferable or cloneable data. Moving work to a worker introduces message and coordination costs, so measure the task before assuming the extra machinery will improve the experience.

Define a message protocol with a request identifier, operation, input, and result or error. Validate incoming messages on both sides. Decide how a worker is terminated and what happens to outstanding requests. Structured cloning and transferable objects have different ownership implications; transferring a buffer can detach it from the sender. Treat message boundaries as real contracts rather than informal calls across a magical background thread.

const worker = new Worker("./analysis-worker.js", { type: "module" });
worker.postMessage({ id: "request-1", type: "analyze", lessons });
// The owning screen must handle replies and terminate the worker on disposal.

Responsive interfaces require resource ownership

Observers, listeners, animation callbacks, media streams, and workers can outlive the screen that created them. Assign an owner and cleanup operation for every resource. Use animation-frame callbacks for visual updates that should coordinate with rendering, while keeping the callback itself small. A timer is not a substitute for a complete animation or scheduling model.

Profile one interaction before and after an improvement. Record the workload, observed main-thread blocking, and user-visible behavior. Test leaving the screen while work is running and returning later. The completed feature should avoid orphaned listeners, stale messages, and repeated initialization. A responsive application is not simply fast on a small fixture; it remains controllable under realistic work and lifecycle changes.

Common pitfalls

  • Using a capability without an unavailable or denied path.
  • Leaving workers, observers, or listeners alive after their owner is disposed.

Retrieve what you learned

1. Can a worker directly update the page DOM?

  1. Yes, with document
  2. No; communicate results to the main thread
  3. Only after setTimeout
  4. Only with innerHTML
Answer and reasoning

B. Workers have a separate context without direct page DOM access.

2. What should an optional capability have?

  1. Only a success demo
  2. Feature detection and a usable fallback
  3. A browser-name guess
  4. A hidden failure
Answer and reasoning

B. Progressive behavior keeps the core task usable across environments.

Practice in your own editor

1. Progressive enhancement

Add a chart or history navigation with a baseline fallback.

Acceptance criteria
  • Essential information remains accessible.
  • Unavailable capability is handled.

2. Worker protocol

Move a measurable calculation behind a worker message interface.

Acceptance criteria
  • Requests have IDs.
  • Errors and cleanup are specified.

3. Lifecycle audit

Navigate away while expensive work is active.

Acceptance criteria
  • Resources are released.
  • Late results cannot corrupt a new screen.

Take it with you

  • Detect capabilities and preserve a baseline.
  • Workers need message contracts.
  • Resources need lifecycle owners.
STAGE 5 / LESSON 30

Browser Application Studio

Ship an accessible learning dashboard with real state and persistence.

Read: Ch. 15 · JavaScript in Web Browsers · Integration studio · Chapter 15
Suggested session: 120 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Integrate rendering, forms, networking, and persistence.
  • Verify complete user flows and failure states.
  • Present a coherent application with an evidence-based review.

Define a complete learner journey

Build a dashboard where a learner browses lessons, filters by stage, plans a session, records completion, and resumes after a reload. Start with a written journey and the states encountered along the way. A successful product slice includes empty results, invalid input, unavailable data, and unsaved changes. These are ordinary parts of using the application, not optional decorations added after the happy path.

Keep curriculum definitions separate from learner progress. Derive summaries from the current model and render them consistently. Give every interactive element a clear purpose and use semantic controls. Choose a visual hierarchy that makes the next useful action obvious, while keeping supporting information available. Attractive styling should reinforce the task flow and readable content rather than compete with it.

Connect boundaries without hiding failures

Wire the domain planner to a browser persistence adapter and a resource-loading adapter. Keep DOM rendering focused on display and event handlers focused on translating user intent. Validate data at boundaries and make asynchronous state explicit. Prevent stale responses from replacing current results, and decide how failed saves affect the visible completion state.

Create a recovery path for malformed saved progress and a retry action for failed loading. Preserve the learner's input where recovery is possible. Test slow responses and rapid repeated actions. If two controls trigger the same domain operation, ensure they share the same validation and state transition instead of maintaining subtly different copies of the business rule.

const state = {
  route: "dashboard",
  load: { status: "idle" },
  progress: { completedIds: [] },
  filters: { stage: "all" }
};

Review the experience with evidence

Run the entire journey using a keyboard, then repeat it with empty data, long titles, a narrow viewport, and controlled request failures. Confirm that focus remains visible, feedback is understandable, and the application resumes correctly after reload. Inspect console errors and verify that resource cleanup prevents duplicate listeners after repeated navigation or remounting.

Score functional correctness at thirty percent, accessibility and interaction at twenty-five, failure handling at twenty-five, and visual clarity at twenty. Deliver the app, run instructions, a scenario checklist, and screenshots of success and recovery states. Record one known limitation honestly. A strong studio is a coherent, usable slice whose claims are supported by repeatable scenarios, not only a polished screenshot taken under ideal conditions. Include a realistic learner fixture in the review so another person can reproduce the complete journey without inventing setup data.

Common pitfalls

  • Polishing only the happy-path screenshot.
  • Duplicating business rules in multiple event handlers.

Retrieve what you learned

1. Which result proves persistence behavior?

  1. A checkbox changes once
  2. Progress survives reload under the documented policy
  3. The page has a logo
  4. A console log says saved
Answer and reasoning

B. Reload exercises the actual persistence contract.

2. What belongs in a browser studio review?

  1. Only desktop screenshots
  2. Full keyboard and failure-state journeys
  3. Only unit tests
  4. Only network speed
Answer and reasoning

B. Usability and resilience require complete interaction scenarios.

Practice in your own editor

1. Working dashboard

Implement browsing, filtering, planning, completion, and resume.

Acceptance criteria
  • Shared domain rules drive every entry point.
  • Progress survives reload.

2. Failure rehearsal

Exercise malformed storage, failed loading, and rapid filter changes.

Acceptance criteria
  • Recovery is actionable.
  • Stale results are prevented.

3. Product review

Deliver a keyboard audit, scenario checklist, and visual evidence.

Acceptance criteria
  • All rubric categories are scored.
  • A narrow viewport remains usable.
  • Known limitations are stated.

Take it with you

  • A product slice includes failure and recovery.
  • Keep rules shared across interactions.
  • Review complete user journeys.
STAGE 6 / LESSON 31

Node.js & Command-Line Programs

Build a useful terminal interface around a reusable core.

Read: Ch. 16 · Server-Side JavaScript with Node · §§16.1–16.2
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Separate Node host APIs from portable JavaScript.
  • Design a CLI with clear input, output, and exit behavior.
  • Keep domain logic reusable across terminal and browser consumers.

Node supplies a different host boundary

Node.js runs JavaScript outside a browser and provides APIs for processes, files, networking, and other system capabilities. The language concepts remain familiar, but document and browser event APIs are not automatically available. A module that performs a calculation can be portable, while a module that reads files needs a Node-specific adapter. Keep that distinction visible in imports and responsibilities.

Inspect a minimal program's arguments, working directory, and environment dependencies. The working directory is not necessarily the directory containing the script, so relative file paths need an explicit policy. Environment variables are strings or absent values, not automatically validated configuration. Parse and validate them at startup, and avoid printing sensitive configuration while debugging. The CLI should explain which inputs it requires without exposing unrelated environment details.

A CLI has a user interface contract

Command-line programs communicate through arguments, standard input, standard output, standard error, and an exit status. Reserve standard output for the requested result when other tools may consume it. Send diagnostics to standard error and set a nonzero exit status when the promised operation fails. A friendly message alone is insufficient if automation sees a successful status for an unsuccessful command.

Define a small command such as plan --minutes 60 --progress progress.json. Specify missing arguments, unknown options, invalid values, and help behavior. Keep machine-readable output separate from decorative progress messages. Test paths containing spaces and execution from another working directory. These cases reveal assumptions that are easy to miss when running only one command manually inside the project folder.

try {
  const options = parseArguments(process.argv.slice(2));
  const result = await runPlanner(options);
  process.stdout.write(JSON.stringify(result) + "\n");
} catch (error) {
  process.stderr.write(error.message + "\n");
  process.exitCode = 1;
}

Keep the core independent of the terminal

The entry point parses arguments, reads required input, invokes the domain planner, and formats the result. The planner should not read process.argv or call process.exit internally. Returning values and throwing meaningful errors lets another consumer use the same core. A boundary handler can map failures to messages and exit behavior while retaining useful diagnostic context for development.

Deliver the CLI with a concise usage guide and examples of successful and rejected commands. Include a structured output mode if another tool will consume the result. Test that a failure does not emit misleading partial success data. The finished program should be useful in a pipeline and understandable to a person, with each output channel serving a deliberate role.

Common pitfalls

  • Assuming the working directory always equals the script directory.
  • Printing an error while returning a successful exit status.

Retrieve what you learned

1. Where should machine-readable results normally go?

  1. Standard error
  2. Standard output
  3. A hidden global
  4. Only the debugger
Answer and reasoning

B. Standard output is the conventional result channel for composition with other tools.

2. Where should process.argv parsing live?

  1. Inside every domain function
  2. At the CLI boundary
  3. In the browser renderer
  4. On Object.prototype
Answer and reasoning

B. Parsing host input at the boundary keeps the core reusable.

Practice in your own editor

1. CLI specification

Define arguments, help, output channels, and exit behavior.

Acceptance criteria
  • Unknown options have a policy.
  • Examples include failure.

2. Planner command

Wrap the existing domain planner in a Node CLI.

Acceptance criteria
  • The core does not read process.argv.
  • Failures set a nonzero status.

3. Invocation matrix

Run from different directories and with paths containing spaces.

Acceptance criteria
  • Path policy is explicit.
  • Structured output remains parseable.

Take it with you

  • Node is a host with its own APIs.
  • A CLI includes channels and exit status.
  • Keep the reusable core independent of process state.
STAGE 6 / LESSON 32

Files, Streams & Backpressure

Process data without assuming it fits in memory.

Read: Ch. 16 · Server-Side JavaScript with Node · §§16.3, 16.5, 16.7
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Choose whole-file or streaming processing deliberately.
  • Explain backpressure as producer-consumer coordination.
  • Handle file errors and cleanup without hiding partial outcomes.

Files are fallible external resources

A file operation can fail because the path is absent, permissions differ, the storage device is unavailable, or the content is malformed. Reading bytes successfully does not validate the data. Keep path selection, byte decoding, parsing, and domain validation as distinct steps. This makes failures easier to diagnose and prevents a low-level error from being mislabeled as an invalid lesson record.

For small bounded files, reading the entire file can be the simplest correct approach. Define the size assumption rather than silently accepting unlimited input. When writing user data, consider how interruption affects the previous file and whether a temporary-file replacement strategy is appropriate. Be precise about guarantees: cross-device operations and platform behavior can affect replacement semantics, so avoid promising universal atomicity without checking the chosen environment.

Streams connect production to consumption

A stream processes chunks over time instead of requiring the entire input at once. Chunks are transport units, not guaranteed logical records. A line or multibyte character can cross chunk boundaries, so decoding and record framing need appropriate handling. Choose established stream and decoder utilities where possible, and test boundaries deliberately rather than assuming one chunk equals one complete JSON object.

Backpressure coordinates a producer with a slower consumer so buffered data does not grow without bound. Respect the stream APIs' signals or use a composition utility that manages them. Streaming does not automatically bound memory if your own code accumulates every chunk in an array. Trace retained data and active work, not just whether the source exposes a stream-shaped interface.

import { pipeline } from "node:stream/promises";
import { createReadStream, createWriteStream } from "node:fs";
await pipeline(
  createReadStream(sourcePath),
  createWriteStream(destinationPath)
);

Failures require end-to-end cleanup

A pipeline connects reading, transformation, and writing. If one stage fails, the others need coordinated termination and cleanup. Use the runtime's pipeline facilities where appropriate rather than wiring only success events. Decide what happens to a partial output file and whether a retry replaces, resumes, or rejects it. The user should be able to distinguish complete output from an interrupted artifact.

Test a slow destination, a malformed record midway through input, a missing file, and an interrupted run. Measure memory with a larger fixture and explain which buffers remain bounded. A correct streaming program should preserve record order when promised, report the source context of failures, and leave resources in a known state. Its value is controlled resource behavior, not merely the presence of stream APIs.

Common pitfalls

  • Assuming a stream chunk is one complete logical record.
  • Accumulating every chunk and then claiming bounded-memory processing.

Retrieve what you learned

1. What is backpressure for?

  1. Encrypting files
  2. Coordinating a producer with consumer capacity
  3. Sorting records
  4. Removing validation
Answer and reasoning

B. Backpressure prevents an uncontrolled producer from overwhelming downstream buffering.

2. Can a line span multiple chunks?

  1. No
  2. Yes
  3. Only in invalid files
  4. Only in browsers
Answer and reasoning

B. Chunk boundaries are not guaranteed to align with logical records.

Practice in your own editor

1. Bounded file loader

Read and validate a small progress file with explicit size assumptions.

Acceptance criteria
  • Missing and malformed files differ.
  • Paths follow a documented policy.

2. Streaming transform

Transform a larger line-oriented fixture without retaining all records.

Acceptance criteria
  • Split records are handled.
  • Order is preserved when promised.

3. Failure and pressure test

Use a slow sink and a midstream error.

Acceptance criteria
  • Cleanup completes.
  • Partial-output policy is visible.
  • Memory behavior is measured.

Take it with you

  • Successful I/O is not successful validation.
  • Chunks are not records.
  • Backpressure and cleanup are end-to-end properties.
STAGE 6 / LESSON 33

HTTP Services & Trust Boundaries

Expose domain behavior through a small, validated service.

Read: Ch. 16 · Server-Side JavaScript with Node · §16.8; review §16.2
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Define HTTP request and response contracts.
  • Validate body size, shape, and domain rules.
  • Handle asynchronous failures without leaking internal details.

HTTP is a protocol boundary

An HTTP service receives a method, target, headers, and an optional body, then produces a status, headers, and a body. Start with a tiny API such as listing lessons and creating a study plan. Define supported methods and paths explicitly. A valid request shape is not enough if its values violate domain rules, so transport parsing and domain validation remain separate responsibilities.

Write example requests and responses before implementation. Include content types, success statuses, invalid-input behavior, unknown routes, and unsupported methods. Keep response shapes consistent so clients do not need to guess whether an error is plain text or JSON. Avoid making every failure a generic success response containing an error field; use the protocol meaningfully and document the chosen contract.

Input is untrusted and resources are finite

Request bodies can be malformed or unexpectedly large. Apply a body-size limit before accumulating unlimited bytes, then parse the supported representation and validate its shape. Do not treat arbitrary paths, headers, or JSON properties as instructions to access files or execute behavior. Keep the service's capabilities narrow and expose only operations that the API intentionally supports.

Validate identifiers and numeric constraints at the boundary, and use the same domain functions as other consumers. Authentication, authorization, and deployment protections require deliberate design when the service moves beyond a local learning environment. For this studio, clearly state the local scope and avoid pretending that a minimal HTTP example is a complete production security architecture. Concrete limits and explicit scope make the exercise honest and useful.

// A boundary sketch: validate before invoking domain behavior.
const input = validatePlanRequest(await readLimitedJson(request));
const result = planSession(input.lessons, input.progress, input.minutes);
response.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "application/json" });
response.end(JSON.stringify(result));

A response has one lifecycle

Asynchronous handlers can fail after parsing or during domain work. Ensure each request reaches one terminal response path and avoid trying to send headers or a second body after completion. Translate internal exceptions into appropriate public errors while retaining diagnostic context on the server. Do not return stack traces or environment details to clients as ordinary error payloads.

Test successful requests, invalid JSON, oversized bodies, unknown routes, and an injected internal failure. Verify status, content type, body shape, and whether the connection completes. Add request identifiers if they help connect a client-visible failure with a diagnostic log, without logging sensitive data unnecessarily. A small service is complete when its failure behavior is as explicit as its successful endpoint example.

Common pitfalls

  • Accumulating request bodies without a size bound.
  • Sending stack traces or attempting a second response after completion.

Retrieve what you learned

1. What should happen before unlimited body accumulation?

  1. Nothing
  2. Apply an explicit size limit
  3. Render a dashboard
  4. Retry parsing forever
Answer and reasoning

B. Input limits protect resource usage before parsing.

2. What should an internal exception expose to a client?

  1. The full environment
  2. An appropriate public error contract
  3. Every stack frame
  4. Server file contents
Answer and reasoning

B. Public errors should be useful without leaking internal diagnostic details.

Practice in your own editor

1. API contract

Specify lesson-list and plan-creation endpoints.

Acceptance criteria
  • Methods, statuses, and shapes are documented.
  • Unknown routes are covered.

2. Validated service

Implement bounded JSON input and shared domain behavior.

Acceptance criteria
  • Malformed and oversized input are rejected.
  • Each request has one response path.

3. Protocol matrix

Exercise success, invalid input, and injected internal failure.

Acceptance criteria
  • Status and content type match the contract.
  • Internal details stay out of public responses.

Take it with you

  • HTTP is an explicit protocol contract.
  • Validate shape, domain rules, and resource limits.
  • Every request needs one complete response lifecycle.
STAGE 6 / LESSON 34

Metaprogramming with Restraint

Understand powerful object hooks and their costs.

Read: Ch. 14 · Metaprogramming · §§14.1–14.4, 14.6–14.7
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Inspect property descriptors and control selected object behavior.
  • Use symbols for protocol participation.
  • Evaluate Proxy and Reflect with invariants and debugging costs.

Properties have behavior beyond values

A property descriptor describes attributes such as writable, enumerable, and configurable, or getter and setter functions. These attributes affect assignment, enumeration, and redefinition. Object.defineProperty creates a property with explicit behavior, and omitted descriptor flags do not all default to permissive values. Inspect descriptors rather than guessing when an assignment or enumeration behaves unexpectedly.

Object.preventExtensions, seal, and freeze impose different restrictions. Freezing an object is shallow: referenced nested objects can remain mutable. It also does not make every resource reachable through an object conceptually immutable. Use these operations when their specific guarantees support a contract, and write an example demonstrating both what is prevented and what remains possible. Overstating the guarantee creates false confidence.

Symbols connect objects to protocols

Symbols can provide property keys that avoid ordinary string-name collisions. Well-known symbols let objects participate in language protocols such as iteration. Implementing Symbol.iterator gives an object a familiar integration point with for...of and other consumers. The value comes from honoring the protocol's behavior, not from making an API obscure or difficult to inspect.

Prefer an explicit method when a protocol hook would surprise callers. A custom conversion behavior can make a simple arithmetic or string operation trigger unexpected work. Keep such hooks predictable and free of unrelated side effects. Document the situations in which the hook runs and test representative language operations so consumers understand the observable consequences of your customization.

const observed = new Proxy(target, {
  get(object, key, receiver) {
    console.log("read", String(key));
    return Reflect.get(object, key, receiver);
  }
});

Proxies require careful semantic boundaries

A Proxy intercepts selected operations through traps, while Reflect offers methods corresponding to fundamental object operations. Forwarding with Reflect can preserve important receiver semantics more accurately than an improvised direct property access. Proxies must also obey language invariants, particularly around nonconfigurable properties. They are not unrestricted permission to redefine every object behavior arbitrarily.

Build a tiny logging or validation proxy, then compare it with an ordinary wrapper function. Measure the added conceptual cost: stack traces, identity, method receivers, private-state interactions, and debugging visibility can become harder to reason about. Choose the proxy only if interception itself is the requirement. For most domain APIs, explicit operations remain easier to discover, test, and explain than invisible behavior attached to ordinary property access. A useful review also demonstrates a case where the simpler explicit wrapper is preferable and explains why interception is unnecessary there.

Common pitfalls

  • Assuming Object.freeze recursively freezes nested objects.
  • Using invisible interception where an explicit operation would be clearer.

Retrieve what you learned

1. What does Object.freeze guarantee about nested objects?

  1. They are all recursively frozen
  2. No automatic recursive freezing
  3. They become strings
  4. They lose their prototypes
Answer and reasoning

B. Freezing is shallow unless additional work recursively freezes references.

2. Why use Reflect inside a proxy trap?

  1. To ignore invariants
  2. To forward a fundamental operation with appropriate semantics
  3. To make code asynchronous
  4. To clone the target
Answer and reasoning

B. Reflect exposes operations designed to correspond to underlying object behavior.

Practice in your own editor

1. Descriptor notebook

Inspect and modify property attributes in small records.

Acceptance criteria
  • Enumeration and assignment outcomes are predicted.
  • Omitted descriptor defaults are observed.

2. Protocol object

Make a custom object iterable using Symbol.iterator.

Acceptance criteria
  • Iteration terminates correctly.
  • Repeated traversal policy is documented.

3. Proxy tradeoff

Implement a narrow observation proxy and an explicit wrapper alternative.

Acceptance criteria
  • Receiver behavior is tested.
  • The chosen approach has a concrete justification.

Take it with you

  • Descriptors control specific property behavior.
  • Protocol hooks must honor predictable contracts.
  • Use interception when interception is the requirement.
STAGE 6 / LESSON 35

Tooling, Testing & Delivery

Create a repeatable path from change to trustworthy release.

Read: Ch. 17 · JavaScript Tools and Extensions · §§17.1–17.5; delivery workshop
Suggested session: 60 minutes

Learning objectives

  • Use project scripts and dependency metadata intentionally.
  • Choose tests according to behavior and risk.
  • Document a reproducible build and delivery workflow.

Tooling should encode the workflow

A project manifest describes scripts and dependencies so another person can reproduce common tasks. Separate development tools from runtime dependencies, and keep the lockfile consistent with the package manager you actually use. A tool is useful when it removes ambiguity or automates a meaningful check. Installing many tools without integrating them into a clear workflow adds maintenance without equivalent confidence.

Provide commands for running, checking, testing, and building where those operations exist. Record the supported runtime and the assumptions required to start from a clean checkout. Linters catch selected patterns; formatters standardize presentation; neither proves domain correctness. A bundler transforms and packages code according to configuration, so verify the built output instead of assuming that a successful development server guarantees a valid release.

Tests should challenge behavior

Choose tests from the contract and likely failure modes.
